ga-static-hq.whatItIs: The recall block matching Indian banks and financial institutions to their headquarters city and their advertising tagline, plus the small set of banking 'firsts' that get asked alongside. Tested only in Mains GA (40 questions, 50 marks, 20 minutes); no Prelims questions. Roughly 4 of the 40 Mains GA questions come from this pool. There is no method to derive an answer — the only skill is storing the discriminating detail so that a five-option set with near-identical distractors resolves in one look.
ga-static-hq.coreMethod:
1. Learn the 12 public sector banks first, as a three-column strip of bank, city and tagline. They generate most of the questions:
   • State Bank of India — Mumbai — 'The Banker to Every Indian' (also uses 'Pure Banking, Nothing Else' and 'With You All The Way')
   • Punjab National Bank — New Delhi (Dwarka) — 'The Name You Can Bank Upon'
   • Bank of Baroda — Vadodara — 'India's International Bank'
   • Bank of India — Mumbai — 'Relationships Beyond Banking'
   • Canara Bank — Bengaluru — 'Together We Can'
   • Union Bank of India — Mumbai — 'Good People to Bank With'
   • Indian Bank — Chennai — 'Your Own Bank'
   • Indian Overseas Bank — Chennai — 'Good People to Grow With'
   • Central Bank of India — Mumbai — 'Central to you Since 1911'
   • UCO Bank — Kolkata — 'Honours Your Trust'
   • Bank of Maharashtra — Pune — 'One Family One Bank'
   • Punjab & Sind Bank — New Delhi — 'Where Service is a Way of Life'
2. For taglines, index on the DISCRIMINATING word — the first word at which a tagline diverges from every other tagline you hold — not on the first word. The headline case proves why: Union Bank of India ('Good People to Bank With') and Indian Overseas Bank ('Good People to Grow With') are identical for three words and identical again at the fourth-from-last; the only cell that separates them is the fourth word, Bank versus Grow. Store the pair as 'Union = Bank, IOB = Grow', then attach the city: Union = Mumbai, IOB = Chennai. Apply the same rule to every near-collision you find; for most taglines the discriminating word happens to be the first word, but you must check rather than assume.
3. Add the private banks as a second strip: HDFC Bank — Mumbai — 'We Understand Your World'; ICICI Bank — Mumbai — 'Khayaal Aapka'; Axis Bank — Mumbai — 'Badhti Ka Naam Zindagi'; Kotak Mahindra Bank — Mumbai — 'Let's Make Money Simple'; IndusInd Bank — Mumbai — 'We Make You Feel Richer'; IDFC First Bank — Mumbai — 'Always You First'; Federal Bank — Aluva, Kerala; South Indian Bank — Thrissur; CSB Bank — Thrissur; Karur Vysya Bank — Karur; City Union Bank — Kumbakonam; Tamilnad Mercantile Bank — Thoothukudi; Karnataka Bank — Mangaluru; Jammu & Kashmir Bank — Srinagar; RBL Bank — Mumbai; Bandhan Bank — Kolkata.
4. Add the institutions, which are asked as often as the banks: NABARD — Mumbai (1982); SIDBI — Lucknow (1990); EXIM Bank — Mumbai (1982); NHB — New Delhi (1988); NaBFID — Mumbai (2021); LIC — Mumbai (1956); SEBI — Mumbai; IRDAI — Hyderabad; PFRDA — New Delhi; IBA — Mumbai; NPCI — Mumbai; DICGC — Mumbai; IBBI — New Delhi.
5. Learn the banking 'firsts' with the exact distinguishing phrase attached, because three of them collide:
   • Bank of Hindostan, 1770 — the first bank in India (long defunct).
   • Bank of Calcutta, 1806 (later Bank of Bengal) — the first Presidency Bank.
   • Oudh Commercial Bank, 1881 — the first bank with limited liability managed by Indians; it failed in 1958.
   • Punjab National Bank, founded 19 May 1894 at Lahore, operations from 12 April 1895 — the first bank started wholly with Indian capital and managed entirely by Indians that still survives today.
   • Central Bank of India, 1911 — the first Indian commercial bank wholly owned AND managed by Indians, and the one described as India's first truly Swadeshi bank.
   The keying discriminator is the stem's phrase, not the concept: 'Swadeshi' points at Central Bank of India; 'limited liability' or 'failed in 1958' points at Oudh Commercial Bank; 'Indian capital and Indian management, still in existence' points at PNB; 'first bank in India' points at Bank of Hindostan. Do not carry both 1894 and 1911 as answers to the same remembered phrase — attach each year to its own phrase and the collision disappears.
6. Revise by covering the CITY column first, because taglines are more distinctive than cities and therefore stick without help. Cities collapse into Mumbai for a large share of the list, which is what makes the non-Mumbai entries — Vadodara, Bengaluru, Chennai, Pune, Kolkata, Lucknow, Hyderabad — the ones actually worth drilling.
7. Note the PNB date pair as a separate line: founded 1894, commenced business 1895. Both years appear in option sets and the stem word 'founded' or 'commenced' decides.
tricks: Drill the non-Mumbai entries only. A large share of the list is headquartered in Mumbai, so the information is carried entirely by the exceptions: Bank of Baroda in Vadodara, Canara in Bengaluru, Indian Bank and IOB in Chennai, UCO and Bandhan in Kolkata, Bank of Maharashtra in Pune, PNB and Punjab & Sind in New Delhi, SIDBI in Lucknow, IRDAI in Hyderabad. Learning eleven exceptions is faster than learning forty entries.

Store each tagline by its discriminating word. Find the first word at which it diverges from every other tagline you hold and index on that word alone. Union Bank indexes on 'Bank' (word four) and IOB on 'Grow' (word four); recalling one word instead of five cuts retrieval time roughly in half and removes the near-collision entirely.

Pair every collision explicitly rather than learning the two entries separately. Union-Mumbai-Bank against IOB-Chennai-Grow, learned as one four-cell unit, is retrieved as one item; learned separately, the two overwrite each other.

On a 'firsts' question, find the qualifying phrase in the stem before you look at the options. 'Swadeshi', 'limited liability', 'still surviving' and 'first bank in India' each point at exactly one institution, and the year in the options follows from the phrase rather than the other way round.

For institution questions, decide first whether the stem wants the city or the founding year. NABARD-Mumbai-1982 and SIDBI-Lucknow-1990 are stored as triples, and reading the stem's noun tells you which cell to pull in about two seconds.

When two options share three or more words of a tagline, that is your signal that the question is testing the collision pair — go straight to the discriminating word instead of reading both options in full.
traps: Storing taglines by their first word. 'Good People to Bank With' (Union Bank of India) and 'Good People to Grow With' (Indian Overseas Bank) share the first three words and the last word; only word four separates them, and a first-word index makes the pair unanswerable.
Placing Bank of Baroda's headquarters in Mumbai. It is Vadodara, even though the bank has a large corporate presence in Mumbai.
Answering Mumbai for SIDBI. SIDBI is headquartered at Lucknow — the single most-missed institution city.

Collapsing the PNB and Central Bank of India firsts into one fact. PNB (1894) is the first bank started with wholly Indian capital and Indian management that still survives; Central Bank of India (1911) is the first Indian commercial bank wholly owned and managed by Indians and is the one described as Swadeshi. The stem's phrase, not the concept, selects between them.
Answering 1895 to 'in which year was Punjab National Bank founded'. It was founded on 19 May 1894 and commenced business on 12 April 1895; both years appear as options and the stem's verb decides.

Confusing Indian Bank with Indian Overseas Bank. Both are headquartered at Chennai but the taglines are different — 'Your Own Bank' against 'Good People to Grow With' — so the city cell cannot separate them and only the tagline can.
Putting IRDAI in New Delhi. IRDAI is at Hyderabad; PFRDA is at New Delhi; SEBI is at Mumbai. All three appear in the same option set on regulator-headquarters items.
ga-static-hq.timeTarget: Mains GA gives 30 seconds per question. An HQ or tagline item should close in 8-12 seconds, because there is nothing to work out — you either hold the cell or you do not, and an item still unresolved at 15 seconds should be left rather than guessed into a 0.25 penalty. Allow up to 20 seconds for a 'firsts' item, where the extra time goes into locating the qualifying phrase in the stem.
ga-static-hq.masteryCheck: In 8 minutes write the three-column strip for all 12 public sector banks — bank, headquarters city and tagline — with no omissions, then add the headquarters city for NABARD, SIDBI, EXIM Bank, NHB, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA. Mastery is 12 out of 12 on the PSB strip with Union Bank and IOB both exactly right, and 7 out of 7 on the institutions. Then answer 15 'firsts' questions, stating the qualifying phrase before the answer; mastery is 14 out of 15. Diagnostic: if you get the city right but the tagline wrong on the Union/IOB pair, you are still indexing on the first word — rebuild that pair as a single four-cell unit.
questionPatterns: 'The tagline Good People to Grow With belongs to which bank?' (a) Union Bank of India (b) Indian Bank (c) Indian Overseas Bank (d) UCO Bank (e) Bank of India. Answer (c) — Union Bank of India uses 'Good People to Bank With'.
'The headquarters of Bank of Baroda is located at:' (a) Mumbai (b) Ahmedabad (c) Vadodara (d) Surat (e) New Delhi. Answer (c).

'Which bank is described as the first Indian commercial bank wholly owned and managed by Indians, and is known as India's first Swadeshi bank?' (a) Punjab National Bank (b) Central Bank of India (c) Oudh Commercial Bank (d) Bank of Hindostan (e) Allahabad Bank. Answer (b) — established 1911.
'Punjab National Bank was founded in which year?' (a) 1881 (b) 1894 (c) 1895 (d) 1906 (e) 1911. Answer (b) — founded 19 May 1894; business commenced 12 April 1895.
'The headquarters of the Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) is at:' (a) Mumbai (b) New Delhi (c) Lucknow (d) Hyderabad (e) Kanpur. Answer (c).
'Which of the following pairs of institution and headquarters is correctly matched?' (a) SEBI — New Delhi (b) IRDAI — Mumbai (c) PFRDA — Hyderabad (d) NABARD — Mumbai (e) NHB — Chennai. Answer (d).
'The tagline One Family One Bank is used by:' (a) Bank of Maharashtra (b) Punjab & Sind Bank (c) Canara Bank (d) Central Bank of India (e) UCO Bank. Answer (a).

ga-static-hq.aiPrompt: You are setting practice for IBPS Clerk Mains 2026 General Awareness, static banking section. Generate 25 questions on the headquarters and taglines of Indian banks and financial institutions. Every question must have exactly FIVE options labelled (a) to (e). Distribute across: headquarters of the 12 public sector banks (6 questions); taglines of the 12 public sector banks (6); headquarters and taglines of major private banks including HDFC, ICICI, Axis, Kotak Mahindra, IndusInd, IDFC First, Federal, South Indian, Karur Vysya, City Union, Karnataka Bank, Jammu & Kashmir Bank and Bandhan (5); headquarters and founding years of institutions — NABARD, SIDBI, EXIM Bank, NHB, NaBFID, LIC, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, NPCI, IBA and DICGC (5); and banking firsts (3). For the firsts, each stem must contain the qualifying phrase that selects the answer — Swadeshi, limited liability, first bank in India, first Presidency Bank, or wholly Indian capital and management still surviving — and Punjab National Bank and Central Bank of India must appear as options in the same set at least once. Include at least one question where Union Bank of India and Indian Overseas Bank are both options and the tagline differs only at one word. Include at least one question where the same city is the answer for two different institutions so the distractors are genuinely hard. In the answer key, state the exact tagline wording and the founding or commencement year, and flag any tagline that a bank has recently changed so I can verify it.
ga-static-hq.blockPlan:
Total build: about 3 hours. Keep it small — this is a tier-4 topic and it should not displace banking awareness or reasoning practice.

Phase 1, one 45-minute session.
20 min: write the 12-row public sector bank strip — bank, city, tagline — on one A4 sheet by hand. Mark the Union Bank / Indian Overseas Bank pair in a box and write the discriminating word beside each.
15 min: 20 MCQs on that strip, untimed, then correct.
10 min: add the eleven non-Mumbai headquarters to a short 'exceptions only' list on the same sheet.

Phase 2, one 40-minute session, two days later.
15 min: add the private banks and the institutions to the reverse of the sheet.
10 min: write the five banking firsts with the qualifying phrase attached to each, not the year.
15 min: 20 mixed MCQs at 25 seconds each, timed, scored with 0.25 negative marking; then correct.

Phase 3, weeks 2-8 — one 12-minute session per week.
4 min covering the CITY column and reciting the exceptions list; 6 min on 15 MCQs; 2 min updating the leak sheet. Do not run 45-question sittings on this topic; the pool of distinct facts is under sixty and a long sitting simply re-asks them.

Phase 4, from October 2026 — one 10-minute session per fortnight, exceptions list and collision pairs only. Check once in November 2026 whether any bank has changed its tagline, which does happen after a rebrand.

Final week before Mains: one 6-minute read of both sides.
ga-static-hq.weightageNote: Bank headquarters and taglines is a Mains-only topic with no Prelims presence, and your planner allots roughly 4 of the 40 Mains GA questions to it — about 5 marks of the 50 that GA contributes to the 200-mark merit total. Note what sectional timing actually implies here: because the 20-minute GA clock cannot be extended and its unused seconds cannot be transferred to any other section, speed has its LOWEST marginal value in GA of anywhere in the paper. The reason to hold these facts is not that they are answered fast but that they are answered without thinking, which leaves your reading capacity free for the banking-awareness and current-affairs items sharing the same 20 minutes. Budget accordingly: about 3 hours of build, then 12 minutes a week.
ga-static-hq.websiteRef: Confirm headquarters and current taglines from each bank's own 'About Us' page rather than from a compiled list — taglines change after a rebrand and compiled lists propagate the old one. For institutions, use nabard.org, sidbi.in, eximbankindia.in, sebi.gov.in, irdai.gov.in and pfrda.org.in.

ga-static-cap.whatItIs: The pure-memory block matching countries to their capital cities and their currencies. Tested only in Mains GA (40 questions, 50 marks, 20 minutes); nothing appears in Prelims. Roughly 4 of the 40 Mains GA questions come from this pool. Zero reasoning is involved: either the pair is in your head or it is not, which makes this the fastest-answering topic in the entire paper and the correct place to bank thinking time for the harder banking and current-affairs items sharing the same 20 minutes.
ga-static-cap.coreMethod:
1. Do not learn 195 countries. Learn four rings and stop: (a) India's nine neighbours, (b) the currency families that generate the confusable options, (c) the multi-capital and non-obvious-capital countries, and (d) any country in the news during your exam window. Everything else is low-yield.
2. Ring A — India's nine neighbours, seven by land and two maritime. Learn each as a triple, country-capital-currency:
   • China — Beijing — Renminbi (the unit is the yuan)
   • Pakistan — Islamabad — Pakistani Rupee
   • Nepal — Kathmandu — Nepalese Rupee
   • Bhutan — Thimphu — Ngultrum
   • Bangladesh — Dhaka — Taka
   • Myanmar — Nay Pyi Taw — Kyat
   • Afghanistan — Kabul — Afghan Afghani
   • Sri Lanka (maritime) — Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte — Sri Lankan Rupee
   • Maldives (maritime) — Malé — Rufiyaa
   China is a neighbour and must be on the list; it is India's second-longest land border after Bangladesh and is asked as often as the rest combined.
3. Ring B — currency families, which is where five-option sets are built:
   • RIYAL, spelt with a y: Saudi Arabia (Riyadh), Qatar (Doha).
   • RIAL, no y: Oman (Muscat), Iran (Tehran), Yemen (Sana'a). Oman's currency is the Omani RIAL — this is the pair most often written wrongly.
   • DINAR: Kuwait (Kuwait City), Bahrain (Manama), Iraq (Baghdad), Jordan (Amman), Algeria (Algiers), Tunisia (Tunis), Libya (Tripoli), Serbia (Belgrade).
   • DIRHAM: United Arab Emirates (Abu Dhabi), Morocco (Rabat).
   • RUPEE / RUPIAH / RUFIYAA: India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Mauritius (Port Louis), Seychelles (Victoria) all use a rupee; Indonesia (Jakarta) uses the RUPIAH; Maldives uses the RUFIYAA. Three different words, one family.
   • PESO: Argentina (Buenos Aires), Chile (Santiago), Colombia (Bogotá), Cuba (Havana), Mexico (Mexico City), Philippines (Manila), Uruguay (Montevideo).
   • KRONE / KRONA: Denmark (Copenhagen) and Norway (Oslo) use the krone; Sweden (Stockholm) uses the krona; Iceland (Reykjavík) uses the króna.
   • POUND: United Kingdom (London), Egypt (Cairo), Sudan (Khartoum), Lebanon (Beirut), Syria (Damascus).
   • Singles worth holding: Türkiye — Ankara — Lira; Japan — Tokyo — Yen; South Korea — Seoul and North Korea — Pyongyang — both Won; Malaysia — Kuala Lumpur — Ringgit; Thailand — Bangkok — Baht; Vietnam — Hanoi — Dong; Cambodia — Phnom Penh — Riel; Laos — Vientiane — Kip; Israel — Jerusalem — Shekel; South Africa — Rand; Nigeria — Abuja — Naira; Kenya — Nairobi — Shilling; Kazakhstan — Astana — Tenge; Russia — Moscow — Rouble; Brazil — Brasília — Real; Timor-Leste — Dili — US Dollar.
4. Ring C — capitals that are not the country's best-known city, plus the multi-capital cases. This is where marks are actually won:
   • Myanmar — Nay Pyi Taw, not Yangon.
   • Sri Lanka — Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte is the official legislative capital; Colombo is the commercial capital and executive seat.
   • Indonesia — Jakarta remains the legal capital as of August 2026. Nusantara was redefined in 2025 as a 'political capital' targeted for 2028, and the Constitutional Court confirmed that Jakarta remains the capital until a presidential decree formally transfers the status.
   • South Africa — three capitals: Pretoria (executive), Cape Town (legislative), Bloemfontein (judicial).
   • Bolivia — Sucre is the constitutional and judicial capital; La Paz is the seat of government.
   • Netherlands — Amsterdam is the constitutional capital; The Hague is the seat of government.
   • Malaysia — Kuala Lumpur is the national capital; Putrajaya is the administrative capital.
   • Tanzania — Dodoma, not Dar es Salaam. Côte d'Ivoire — Yamoussoukro, not Abidjan. Nigeria — Abuja, not Lagos.
   • Türkiye — Ankara, not Istanbul. Australia — Canberra, not Sydney. Canada — Ottawa, not Toronto. Switzerland — Bern, not Zurich or Geneva. Brazil — Brasília, not Rio de Janeiro. New Zealand — Wellington, not Auckland. USA — Washington D.C., not New York.
5. Ring D — any country that appeared in the news during your window. Timor-Leste (Dili, US Dollar) is the live example, having become ASEAN's eleventh member on 26 October 2025.
6. Revise by covering the CURRENCY column first, then the CAPITAL column. Capitals stick faster than currencies, so the currency column needs the extra pass.
7. Re-verify Ring C once in November 2026. Capital-city status changes by legislation and a stale note here is invisible until it costs you a mark.
tricks: Spell-check the Gulf pair before answering. Saudi Arabia and Qatar use the RIYAL with a y; Oman, Iran and Yemen use the RIAL without one. A five-option set will put both spellings in front of you, so read the option letter by letter rather than by shape.

Answer by family, not by country. If you know a country sits in the dinar family, you have eliminated every option offering a riyal, dirham or peso in about two seconds without recalling the specific currency.

For multi-capital countries, read the stem's adjective first. 'Legislative capital of South Africa' is Cape Town, 'executive' is Pretoria, 'judicial' is Bloemfontein — and the same technique answers Bolivia, the Netherlands and Sri Lanka. Without the adjective the item is unanswerable, so look for it before you look at the options.

Store the nine neighbours as one recited chain in geographical order — Pakistan, Afghanistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, then Sri Lanka and Maldives across the water. Reciting the chain surfaces the whole set in about six seconds and stops you dropping China, which is the neighbour most often left off a memorised list.

Attach the currency to a phonetic hook where one exists and skip the hook where it does not. Bhutan-Ngultrum and Maldives-Rufiyaa have no confusable neighbours, so learn them flat; the Gulf and Scandinavian sets are where hooks actually pay.

When two cities from the same country appear as options, the item is almost certainly testing a not-the-obvious-city capital. That is a signal to slow down for five seconds rather than to answer on instinct — it is the exact configuration where the well-known commercial city is the wrong answer.
traps: Writing Oman's currency as the Riyal. It is the Omani RIAL. Saudi Arabia and Qatar take the y; Oman, Iran and Yemen do not.
Leaving China out of India's neighbours. India has nine neighbours — seven land and two maritime — and China (Beijing, Renminbi) is one of them. A memorised list of eight is a list missing China.
Answering Colombo for the capital of Sri Lanka. The official capital is Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte; Colombo is the commercial capital. Both appear in the same option set.

Answering Nusantara for Indonesia's capital. As of August 2026 Jakarta remains the legal capital; Nusantara was redefined in 2025 as a political capital targeted for 2028 and the status transfer requires a presidential decree that has not been issued.
Answering Yangon for Myanmar. The capital was moved to Nay Pyi Taw; Yangon is the largest city.
Giving one capital for South Africa. It has three, each with a distinct function, and the stem will name the function.
Reading Indonesia's currency as the rupee. Indonesia uses the RUPIAH and the Maldives uses the RUFIYAA; only India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Mauritius and Seychelles use a rupee.
Treating Sweden, Norway and Denmark as identical. Denmark and Norway use the krone; Sweden uses the krona. The single letter is the whole question.
ga-static-cap.timeTarget: Mains GA gives 30 seconds per question. A capital-or-currency item is pure retrieval and should close in 8-12 seconds — if the pair is not in your head by then it will not arrive at 25 seconds, so leave it rather than pay 0.25. Allow 15-20 seconds for a multi-capital item, where the extra time goes into reading the stem's adjective. The point of finishing these fast is not to finish the section early: GA is sectionally timed and banked seconds are stranded, so redirect the surplus into the banking-awareness and current-affairs questions in the same 20 minutes, which reward a second reading.
ga-static-cap.masteryCheck: In 5 minutes write all nine of India's neighbours with capital AND currency for each, with China present. Then, in 6 minutes, write the currency for 30 countries drawn from the four rings, with correct spelling — riyal versus rial and krone versus krona both count as errors when wrong. Mastery is 27 or better out of 30 with all nine neighbours perfect. Diagnostic: if your errors are concentrated in spelling rather than in recall, drill only the riyal/rial, krone/krona and rupee/rupiah/rufiyaa triples for three days rather than re-reading the whole list.
questionPatterns: 'The currency of Oman is the:' (a) Omani Riyal (b) Omani Rial (c) Omani Dinar (d) Omani Dirham (e) Omani Pound. Answer (b).

'Which of the following pairs of country and capital is correctly matched?' (a) Myanmar — Yangon (b) Sri Lanka — Colombo (c) Bhutan — Thimphu (d) Australia — Sydney (e) Türkiye — Istanbul. Answer (c).
'Beijing is the capital of China. What is China's currency called?' (a) Yen (b) Won (c) Renminbi (d) Ringgit (e) Tenge. Answer (c) — the unit of the renminbi is the yuan.
'Which city is the legislative capital of South Africa?' (a) Pretoria (b) Johannesburg (c) Bloemfontein (d) Cape Town (e) Durban. Answer (d).

'As of 2026, what is the legal capital of Indonesia?' (a) Nusantara (b) Jakarta (c) Surabaya (d) Bandung (e) Medan. Answer (b) — Jakarta remains the capital until a presidential decree transfers the status.
'The currency of the Maldives is the:' (a) Maldivian Rupee (b) Rupiah (c) Rufiyaa (d) Ringgit (e) Riel. Answer (c).
'Which of the following countries does NOT share a land border with India?' (a) Bhutan (b) Myanmar (c) Afghanistan (d) Maldives (e) Nepal. Answer (d) — the Maldives is a maritime neighbour only.

ga-static-cap.blockPlan:
Total build: about 3.5 hours. This is a low-tier topic — do not let it eat time that belongs to banking awareness or reasoning.

Phase 1, one 45-minute session.
15 min: write Ring A, India's nine neighbours, as nine triples on one A4 sheet. Recite the chain aloud five times.
20 min: write Ring B, the currency families, grouped by family with the capitals attached, on the same sheet.
10 min: 15 MCQs on Rings A and B, untimed, then correct.

Phase 2, one 40-minute session, two days later.
20 min: write Ring C — the non-obvious capitals and the multi-capital countries with their functions — on the reverse.
12 min: 20 MCQs across all three rings at 30 seconds each, timed, scored with 0.25 negative marking.
8 min: correction, and every miss onto the leak sheet.

Phase 3, weeks 2-8 — one 12-minute session per week.
4 min covering the CURRENCY column and reciting; 6 min on 15 MCQs; 2 min updating the leak sheet. Twelve minutes is the right size — this topic does not reward 40-question sittings, because past about 15 items you are re-testing the same families.

Phase 4, from October 2026 — one 10-minute session per fortnight, leak sheet only, plus a single 10-minute check in November 2026 to re-verify Ring C against a current source, since capital-city status changes by legislation.

Final week before Mains: one 6-minute read of both sides of the A4 sheet.
ga-static-cap.weightageNote: Capitals and currencies is a Mains-only topic with no Prelims presence. Your planner allots roughly 4 of the 40 Mains GA questions to it — a small share of the 50 GA marks, and a small share of the 200 that decide merit. It is placed in tier 4 for a reason: the marks are real but few, and the honest budget is about 3.5 hours of build plus 12 minutes a week, not a memorisation project. Its value is that these questions cost almost no thinking time inside a 20-minute sectional clock, which leaves reading capacity for the banking-awareness items in the same section.
ga-static-cap.websiteRef: For capital-city status and official currency names, check the country's entry on mea.gov.in (Ministry of External Affairs country briefs) and, for currency spelling and codes, the ISO 4217 currency list published at iso.org. Coaching lists reproduce spelling errors between themselves; a primary source settles riyal versus rial in one look.

ga-days.whatItIs: Dated observances — international days declared by the UN and its agencies, and national days declared by the Government of India — together with the annual theme attached to the larger ones. Two facts are examinable per day: the date, which is permanent, and the theme, which changes every year. A third is examinable for a few days only: the host country, which rotates. The date half is completely static and can be locked for good; the theme half is a small maintenance job that only makes sense for the fifteen or so days whose themes are actually publicised. It is the smallest tier-4 block in GA, but it is also the cheapest per mark in the whole section because almost every fact is a two-item pair with nothing to derive.
ga-days.coreMethod:
1. LEARN DATES BY MONTH BLOCK, NOT AS AN ALPHABETICAL LIST. Take one month at a time, write every observance in that month on a single line in date order, and drill the month as a unit. Twelve small lists are learnable; one list of 150 items is not. Two months per study session gets the whole year in six sessions.

2. ATTACH EVERY DATE TO THE EVENT IT COMMEMORATES. A date with a reason behind it is a fact you can rebuild; a bare date is a fact you can only lose. The founding anchors: 7 April, World Health Day, marks the founding of the WHO in 1948. 16 October, World Food Day, marks the founding of the FAO in 1945. 24 October, United Nations Day, marks the UN Charter coming into force in 1945. 10 December, Human Rights Day, marks the adoption of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. 20 November, World Children's Day, marks the adoption of the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1989.

3. USE BIRTHDAYS FOR THE INDIAN NATIONAL DAYS — ALMOST ALL OF THEM ARE ONE. 12 January, National Youth Day, Swami Vivekananda. 28 February, National Science Day, the announcement of the Raman effect in 1928. 29 June, National Statistics Day, P. C. Mahalanobis. 1 July, National Doctors' Day, Dr B. C. Roy. 5 September, Teachers' Day, Dr S. Radhakrishnan. 15 September, Engineers' Day, Sir M. Visvesvaraya. 31 October, National Unity Day, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. 14 November, Children's Day, Jawaharlal Nehru. 22 December, National Mathematics Day, Srinivasa Ramanujan. Also 11 May, National Technology Day, marking the Pokhran-II tests of 1998, and 26 November, Constitution Day, marking the adoption of the Constitution in 1949.

4. LEARN CONFUSABLE PAIRS TOGETHER, NEVER APART. The exam's whole design in this topic is to place two similarly named days in the same option set, so the pair is the unit of learning. World Water Day 22 March and World Meteorological Day 23 March. World Consumer Rights Day 15 March and National Consumer Rights Day, India, 24 December. World Food Safety Day 7 June and World Food Day 16 October. World Environment Day 5 June, World Nature Conservation Day 28 July and World Ozone Day 16 September. World Health Day 7 April, International Nurses Day 12 May and National Doctors' Day 1 July. National Statistics Day 29 June and World Statistics Day 20 October. International Women's Day 8 March, National Girl Child Day, India, 24 January, and the International Day of the Girl Child 11 October. International Literacy Day 8 September and National Education Day, India, 11 November. National Science Day 28 February, National Technology Day 11 May and the World Science Day for Peace and Development 10 November.

5. SEPARATE THE HEALTH-DAY CLUSTER EXPLICITLY. World Cancer Day 4 February, World TB Day 24 March, World Health Day 7 April, World Malaria Day 25 April, International Nurses Day 12 May, World Blood Donor Day 14 June, and World AIDS Day 1 December. Seven dates spread across the year that all read as generic health observances — they need one dedicated drill of their own or they collapse into each other.

6. HANDLE THEMES AS SHORT STRINGS, AND ONLY FOR THE BIG FIFTEEN. Store the first three or four words, not the full sentence; that is all a five-option question needs to distinguish. Verified 2026 themes worth holding: World Water Day, 22 March — 'Water and Gender', campaign line 'Where water flows, equality grows'. World Health Day, 7 April — 'Together for health. Stand with science'. International Day of Yoga, 21 June — 'Yoga for Healthy Ageing'. World Population Day, 11 July — 'Realizing the hopes and aspirations of young people'. Pull the remaining 2026 themes from the UN observances page and each agency's own site, not from aggregator blogs, which routinely carry a previous year's theme under the current year's heading.

7. STORE THE ROTATING HOST WHERE ONE EXISTS. World Environment Day has a different global host country every year; the 2026 commemoration is hosted by Azerbaijan, in Baku. Host country and theme are two separate examinable fields for the same day, and a stem asks for exactly one of them — confirm the exact 2026 theme wording on unep.org before committing it.

8. DRILL IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, TIMED. Give yourself fifteen dates and write the day; then fifteen day-names and write the date. Both directions are asked and the second is harder, because dates are what you rehearsed. Three minutes per direction.

9. RE-TEST WEEKLY AT FOUR MINUTES, THEN LET IT GO. Once you clear both directions cleanly twice, drop the date half to a monthly check and spend the saved time on the theme half, which is the only part that decays.
tricks: Rebuild rather than recall by storing the commemorated event alongside the date. If you know World Food Day marks the FAO's founding, you can reconstruct 16 October even after the bare date has faded, and a date you can reconstruct never fully leaves. Bare dates fade to nothing.

Chunk by month and always drill the month in date order. Twelve lists of ten to fifteen items each are within working memory; a single undifferentiated list of 150 is not, and the difference is entirely in how you organised it, not in how hard you worked.

Store themes as their first three or four words only. Five options for a theme question differ from each other within the opening phrase, so the rest of the sentence is storage you pay for and never use. This roughly triples the number of themes you can carry.

Learn every 'World X Day' with its 'National X Day, India' twin in the same breath — consumer rights, statistics, education, girl child. These pairs exist specifically to be confused, and a pair learned as a pair costs almost nothing more than one learned alone.

Keep a one-line note of which days have a rotating host country. It is a very short list, and it tells you instantly whether 'host country' is even a valid question for the day in the stem, which kills options rather than weighing them.
traps: World Food Day, 16 October, versus World Food Safety Day, 7 June. One word apart, four months apart, different UN anchors — 16 October marks the founding of the FAO in 1945. Both appear in the same option set and the stem is read too fast to notice which one it named.

World Consumer Rights Day, 15 March, versus National Consumer Rights Day in India, 24 December. The word 'World' or 'National' is the entire content of the question. The same structure recurs with Statistics Day, 29 June in India against World Statistics Day on 20 October, and with Education and Literacy Day.

The health-day cluster. World Health Day on 7 April marks the founding of the WHO in 1948; International Nurses Day on 12 May is anchored to Florence Nightingale's birth; National Doctors' Day in India on 1 July is anchored to Dr B. C. Roy. All three read as 'a health day' and options will offer all three dates for any one of them. There is no shortcut — the anchor is what separates them.

National Science Day, 28 February, versus National Technology Day, 11 May. Both are Indian, both scientific, and each has a distinct anchor: the Raman effect announcement of 1928 and the Pokhran-II tests of 1998. Aspirants who memorised only 'science-related Indian day' cannot separate them under time pressure.

Theme asked when you learned the host, or the reverse. For World Environment Day both are examinable and both change annually — Azerbaijan hosts the 2026 commemoration in Baku, and the theme is a separate string. Read whether the stem says 'theme' or 'host country' before scanning the options.

A theme from the previous year presented as this year's. Aggregator sites are unreliable on themes specifically, and a theme that circulated widely twelve months ago will feel familiar and correct. Confirm every theme on un.org, who.int or the relevant agency's own page before it enters your notes.
ga-days.timeTarget: 8–15 seconds per question. Both halves of the topic are pure two-item recall with nothing to work out; if you are past 15 seconds you are choosing between two dates rather than remembering one, and a blank beats that choice under 0.25 negative marking.
ga-days.masteryCheck: Two timed directions in one sitting. First, given 15 dates drawn from across all twelve months, write the observance for each — pass at 14 out of 15 in under three minutes. Second, given 15 observance names, write the dates — pass at 13 out of 15 in under three minutes, since this direction is genuinely harder. Then separately write the four verified 2026 themes and the World Environment Day host country from memory. You own the date half permanently once you clear both directions twice at least a week apart; the theme half needs a five-minute refresh each month up to December.
questionPatterns: Date recall: 'World Food Day is observed every year on — (a) 7 June (b) 11 July (c) 16 September (d) 16 October (e) 24 October'. Answer (d), marking the founding of the FAO in 1945.

Reverse direction: 'Which day is observed on 29 June in India? (a) National Doctors\' Day (b) National Statistics Day (c) World Statistics Day (d) National Science Day (e) International Day of Yoga'. Answer (b), anchored to P. C. Mahalanobis.

Theme: 'The theme of World Health Day 2026 was — (a) Healthy Beginnings, Hopeful Futures (b) Together for health. Stand with science (c) My Health, My Right (d) Our Planet, Our Health (e) Health for All'. Answer (b); the distractors are themes from earlier years, which is exactly how this question type is built.
Host country: 'Which country hosted the global commemoration of World Environment Day 2026? (a) India (b) Saudi Arabia (c) Azerbaijan (d) Brazil (e) Côte d\'Ivoire'. Answer (c), in Baku.

Anchor question: 'National Technology Day in India commemorates — (a) the announcement of the Raman effect (b) the launch of Aryabhata (c) the Pokhran-II nuclear tests of 1998 (d) the founding of ISRO (e) the first flight of the indigenous Tejas'. Answer (c), which is why it falls on 11 May.

Match-the-following: five observances against five dates with five permutation options (a) to (e), typically mixing one confusable pair such as World Consumer Rights Day and National Consumer Rights Day into the same set.
ga-days.searchQuery: international days observances list with themes 2026 site:un.org
ga-days.aiPrompt:
You are building General Awareness practice on important days and themes for IBPS Clerk Mains 2026. Do not ask me for any input before you begin.

STEP 1 — Print a month-by-month table of observances, January to December, with columns: Date | Observance | International or Indian national | What it commemorates | 2026 theme, where one is officially published | Host country, where one rotates. Include at least 90 observances. Tag any theme you are not certain belongs to 2026 rather than an earlier year with [VERIFY] and name the official page to check (un.org, who.int, unep.org, unfpa.org or the relevant agency's own site). Themes are the single least reliable field in this topic — be conservative about which ones you leave untagged.

STEP 2 — Print a separate table of CONFUSABLE PAIRS: every case where two observances share most of a name, or where a 'World' day has an Indian 'National' counterpart on a different date. Give both dates side by side and one line on what distinguishes them. Cover at minimum: World and National Consumer Rights Day, World and National Statistics Day, World Food Day and World Food Safety Day, World Health Day and International Nurses Day and National Doctors' Day, National Science Day and National Technology Day, International Literacy Day and National Education Day, World Environment Day and World Ozone Day and World Nature Conservation Day, International Women's Day and National Girl Child Day and International Day of the Girl Child.

STEP 3 — Write 20 multiple-choice questions. HARD FORMAT RULE: exactly FIVE options labelled (a) to (e) on every question, without exception. IBPS Clerk papers carry five options — never write four. Compose the set as: 6 date-recall questions, 5 reverse-direction questions giving the date and asking the observance, 3 theme questions using untagged themes only and with earlier-year themes as the distractors, 2 host-country questions, 2 commemoration-anchor questions, and 2 five-row match-the-following questions with permutation options. At least four questions must place a confusable pair from Step 2 inside the same option set.

STEP 4 — Answer key with one line each naming the date, the anchor event where there is one, and for the confusable-pair questions the date of the day that was NOT the answer.

STEP 5 — Reprint every [VERIFY] theme as a checklist headed 'Confirm these on the official site before memorising'.

Do not include guessing heuristics, elimination-by-frequency rules, or any 'the answer is usually' statement.
ga-days.blockPlan: Six sessions of 30 minutes each, two months of the calendar per session, fitted inside your 45-minute GA block alongside a shorter second topic. In each session: write the month's observances in date order, add the commemoration anchor for every day that has one, and finish with a two-minute both-directions drill on that month. After the sixth session, run one full-year drill of both directions at 6 minutes total. Then drop to a 4-minute weekly re-test for three weeks, and once you have cleared the mastery check twice, move the date half to a monthly check. Keep a separate 5-minute monthly slot for themes only — themes are the sole part of this topic that decays, and they should be re-pulled from official sources in late November so what you carry into 27 December is current. Whole-topic first-pass cost is about three and a half hours, which is the smallest total in the GA plan.
ga-days.weightageNote: Zero in Prelims, which has no GA section. In Mains, GA is 40 questions for 50 marks in 20 minutes, and this plan budgets roughly 4 questions to important days — a tier-4 allocation and one of the smaller blocks in the section. What justifies the slot is cost rather than count: the first pass is about three and a half hours, almost all of it permanent, and each question resolves in ten to fifteen seconds with no working. Schedule it in gaps rather than against a large block, and never let it displace the current-affairs register, which carries several times the marks.

ga-awards.whatItIs: Two quite different things sold under one heading. The first is static: which body confers each award, in which field, on what calendar rhythm, and what it replaced or was renamed from. That half never changes and can be finished once. The second is dynamic: this year's winners, which churn and must be maintained inside a rolling six-month window against a 27 December Mains. Examinable awards span civilian honours (Bharat Ratna, the three Padma grades), gallantry decorations, sports awards, literature prizes, film awards, science awards, and the international set led by the six Nobel Prizes. Treating the static and dynamic halves as one topic is the standard mistake — it makes the finishable part feel endless and the churning part feel finished.
ga-awards.coreMethod:
1. SPLIT THE TOPIC IN TWO BEFORE YOU STUDY ANY OF IT. Sheet A is static: award name, conferring body, field, announcement month, conferment month, former name if renamed. Sheet B is the six-month winner register. Sheet A is built once and archived; Sheet B is maintained weekly. Different sheets, different revision rates.

2. BUILD SHEET A FIRST AND COMPLETELY. Civilian: Bharat Ratna and Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, Padma Shri — all conferred by the President, announced on the eve of Republic Day, and actually conferred at Rashtrapati Bhavan ceremonies usually in March or April. Gallantry, wartime: Param Vir Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra, Vir Chakra. Gallantry, peacetime: Ashoka Chakra, Kirti Chakra, Shaurya Chakra — announced on Republic Day and Independence Day. Sports: Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna (the highest, renamed from Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna in 2021), Arjuna Award (for a player's performance over years), Dronacharya Award (for coaches), Dhyan Chand Award (lifetime achievement by a player), Rashtriya Khel Protsahan Puraskar (for organisations), Maulana Abul Kalam Azad Trophy (for universities). Literature: Jnanpith, conferred by the Bharatiya Jnanpith trust — not by the Government; Sahitya Akademi Award, by the national academy of letters; Vyas Samman and Saraswati Samman, both by the K. K. Birla Foundation. Cinema: National Film Awards and the Dadasaheb Phalke Award within them, by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. Science: the Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar scheme, with its four categories Vigyan Ratna, Vigyan Shri, Vigyan Yuva–Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar, and Vigyan Team. International: the six Nobel Prizes (Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine, Literature, Peace, and the Economics prize established by the Sveriges Riksbank), plus Ramon Magsaysay, Abel Prize, Fields Medal, Pritzker, Gandhi Peace Prize (Ministry of Culture) and the Indira Gandhi Prize for Peace, Disarmament and Development.

3. STORE EACH SHEET A ENTRY AS A THREE-PART TRIPLET: award, conferring body, field. Say them as one string — 'Jnanpith, Bharatiya Jnanpith trust, literature'; 'Dadasaheb Phalke, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, cinema'. The conferring body is the field most often manipulated in options and the cheapest to store, so make it part of the award's name in your head rather than a separate lookup.

4. ANCHOR SHEET A BY ANNOUNCEMENT MONTH. January: Padma awards on Republic Day eve; Republic Day gallantry list. August: Independence Day gallantry list. October: the Nobel announcements, one category per day across the first two weeks. Calendar anchoring means that when a question mentions a month you have already narrowed the award family before reading the options.

5. LOCK THE NUMBERS THAT ARE ASKED AS NUMBERS. Bharat Ratna: a maximum of three in a single year, and since the 2011 amendment it may be awarded for achievement in any field of human endeavour, not only arts, literature, science and public service. Nobel: six prizes, and there is NO Nobel Prize in Mathematics. Padma awards for 2026: 131 recipients in all — 5 Padma Vibhushan, 13 Padma Bhushan, 113 Padma Shri, including 19 women, 6 in the foreigners/NRI/PIO/OCI category and 16 posthumous. Counts like these are directly examinable and cost seconds to store.

6. BUILD SHEET B FROM A SINGLE SOURCE, IN ONE FORMAT. Award | Winner | Field or category | Date announced | Previous year's winner. Six months back from the exam means your live window on 27 December runs roughly from July 2026. Use one monthly current-affairs compilation as the source — using three sources creates three inconsistent registers and no confidence in any of them.

7. CROSS-LINK EVERY WINNER TO THEIR OTHER IDENTITY. A Padma Bhushan recipient is also a cricketer, an industrialist or a musician; a Nobel laureate has a nationality and an institution. Questions frequently approach the person from the other direction — 'which award was conferred on the industrialist X' — so store the person's principal identity in the same row.

8. MAINTAIN AND PRUNE WEEKLY. Twenty minutes a week: add the week's awards, drop rows that have aged out of the six-month window, and re-read the last four weeks. From 1 December, stop adding and consolidate.

9. DRILL BY COVERING THE WINNER COLUMN. Recover winner from award, then award from winner. Two passes over Sheet B takes about four minutes. Reading the register end to end does not build the recall you need in a 20-minute GA section.

10. VERIFY ANY WINNER YOU ARE ABOUT TO COMMIT TO MEMORY. Award-year confusion is endemic in secondary sources, and a laureate list from the previous cycle circulates widely mislabelled with the current year. Check the awarding body's own site — nobelprize.org, padmaawards.gov.in, the relevant ministry's PIB release — before a name enters Sheet B. A wrong row is worse than an empty one, because you will answer confidently and lose 1.25 marks against the correct answer.
tricks: Split static from dynamic on physically separate sheets. Roughly half the marks in this topic come from facts that have not changed in decades, and mixing them with the churning winner list means you re-read stable material every week for no return while the volatile material gets the same insufficient attention.

Encode the conferring body inside the award's name at first learning: 'Jnanpith-of-the-Bharatiya-Jnanpith-trust', 'Gandhi-Peace-Prize-of-the-Ministry-of-Culture'. Body-mismatch is the most common way an otherwise correct-looking option is wrong, and building the body into the name means you never have to make a second retrieval under time pressure.

Group awards into families of three and store the family, not the members: three Padma grades, three wartime gallantry decorations, three peacetime gallantry decorations, three sports awards for individuals (Khel Ratna, Arjuna, Dhyan Chand). Recalling a family of three is one retrieval instead of three.

Store renamed awards as a pair with the year of renaming — 'Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna, renamed 2021, formerly Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna'. The old name still appears in option sets and in older practice material, so the pair is what you actually need.

Flag posthumous awards in the register with a single marker. Questions ask specifically which awards were conferred posthumously, and the marker turns a fact you already stored into a second answerable fact at no extra cost.
traps: Dadasaheb Phalke Award versus the Dadasaheb Phalke International Film Festival Award. The first is the Government's highest cinema honour, conferred as part of the National Film Awards by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. The second is a privately run festival prize with a nearly identical name and different recipients. Options place both, and only the ministry's award is the answer to a stem about the national honour.

Announced versus conferred, for the Padma awards. They are announced on the eve of Republic Day in January but actually conferred at Rashtrapati Bhavan ceremonies usually in March or April. A stem asking when the awards were conferred wants the spring date, not 26 January, and both months will be among the five options.

Bharat Ratna treated as a Padma award. It is a separate and higher civilian honour, capped at three in a year, and since 2011 open to any field of human endeavour. An option describing it as the highest of the Padma awards, or restricting it to arts, literature, science and public service, is wrong on both counts.

Arjuna versus Dronacharya versus Dhyan Chand. Arjuna goes to a player for consistent performance over years; Dronacharya goes to a coach; the Dhyan Chand Award is for lifetime achievement by a player. A question naming a coach and offering all three has exactly one right answer, and the three are so often listed together that they blur.

Nobel Prize in Mathematics. There is none — the six categories are Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine, Literature, Peace, and the Economics prize instituted by the Sveriges Riksbank in memory of Alfred Nobel. Mathematics is covered by the Abel Prize (annual) and the Fields Medal (every four years, to mathematicians under 40). Any option offering a Nobel in Mathematics is wrong on definition.

Jnanpith treated as a Government award. It is conferred by the Bharatiya Jnanpith, a trust. The Government's national literary honour is the Sahitya Akademi Award. Options swap the two conferring bodies while keeping the award names correct.
ga-awards.timeTarget: 10–20 seconds for a static-half question, 15–25 seconds for a winner question. Beyond 25 seconds you are choosing between two names rather than recalling one, and with 0.25 negative marking a blank is better than a coin-flip between two of five options.
ga-awards.masteryCheck: Two separate passes. Static: on a blank sheet in under six minutes, write every award family with its conferring body, field and announcement month — civilian, both gallantry sets, all six sports awards, the four literature prizes, the film awards, the four Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar categories, and the six Nobel categories with an explicit note that Mathematics is not among them. Dynamic: cover the winner column of Sheet B and recover at least 85 percent of the winners from the award name in four minutes, then reverse the direction. You own the static half permanently once you clear it twice a week apart; the dynamic half never stays owned, so it needs the weekly loop through December.
questionPatterns: Conferring body: 'The Jnanpith Award is conferred by — (a) the Ministry of Culture (b) the Sahitya Akademi (c) the Bharatiya Jnanpith trust (d) the President of India (e) the K. K. Birla Foundation'. Answer (c).

Category discrimination: 'The Dronacharya Award is given for — (a) lifetime achievement by a player (b) outstanding coaching in sports (c) consistent performance by a player over four years (d) promotion of sports by a corporate body (e) the best performing university in inter-university tournaments'. Answer (b).

Count recall: 'The Padma Awards for 2026 were announced for how many recipients in total? (a) 106 (b) 113 (c) 128 (d) 131 (e) 139'. Answer (d) — 5 Padma Vibhushan, 13 Padma Bhushan and 113 Padma Shri; 113 is planted as a distractor because it is the Padma Shri count.
Definitional exclusion: 'The Nobel Prize is NOT awarded in which of the following fields? (a) Chemistry (b) Literature (c) Mathematics (d) Peace (e) Physiology or Medicine'. Answer (c).

Winner-to-award: a stem naming a person and asking which honour was conferred on them in the current cycle, with five awards as options. Build this direction into Sheet B drills, because the register is naturally stored the other way round.

Match-the-following: five awards matched against five conferring bodies, with five permutation options (a) to (e). This is the standard format for the static half and is why the award-to-body triplet has to be a single stored string rather than two separate facts.
ga-awards.searchQuery: awards and honours last six months India national international current affairs site:pib.gov.in

ga-awards.blockPlan: Front-load the static half, then run the dynamic half as a small weekly cost. Week 1: two 45-minute GA blocks to build and drill Sheet A completely, ending each with a blank-sheet reproduction — after these two sessions roughly half the topic is permanently yours. From week 2 onwards: a fixed 20-minute slot each week inside your GA block, sharing the same session as the appointments register since both draw from the same monthly compilation — 10 minutes to add and prune Sheet B, 10 minutes to run the cover-the-column drill in both directions. Re-test Sheet A for 5 minutes once a month, no more. From 1 December stop adding to Sheet B and spend the weekly slot consolidating what is already there, because a fact added in the last three weeks is unlikely to survive to 27 December while a fact drilled four times will.

In Mains, GA is 40 questions for 50 marks in 20 minutes; this plan budgets roughly 23 Mains questions to the tier-1 current-affairs cluster, and awards is one of its larger components alongside appointments, summits and schemes. ga-appointments.whatItIs: Who currently holds which post, when they took it, whom they replaced, and where they sit in the numbered sequence of holders. Three layers get asked: national constitutional and statutory posts (CJI, CEC, CAG, Governors of states, service chiefs, heads of RBI/SEBI/IRDAI/NABARD and public sector banks), heads of international bodies (UN, IMF, World Bank, WTO, WHO, ADB, AIIB, NDB), and soft appointments (brand ambassadors, goodwill ambassadors, chairs of newly formed committees). It is the most volatile block in the whole GA section: the fact set turns over monthly, so a register built in August and never touched again will be materially wrong by 27 December. It is also, separately, a static-tenure topic — the number of years a post is held for is fixed by law for some posts and set case-by-case for others, and confusing the two is the defect that costs marks.
ga-appointments.coreMethod:
1. ANCHOR THE WINDOW TO THE EXAM, NOT TO TODAY. Mains is 27 December 2026. IBPS current-affairs questions in practice draw from roughly the six months preceding the paper, with a cut-off a few weeks before it. So your live window on exam day is approximately July to early December 2026. Build the register from 1 June 2026 onward and let the front edge roll forward each week. Every time you revise, re-check that your oldest entries are still inside the window — an appointment from March 2026 is static background by December, not current affairs.

2. USE ONE ENTRY FORMAT FOR EVERY ROW, WITH NO EXCEPTIONS. Post | Name | Ordinal (e.g. 53rd) | Date announced/appointed | Date took charge | Predecessor. Six fields, one line. The format matters more than the content because every question type maps onto one field, and a register with ragged rows cannot be drilled.

3. SPLIT THE REGISTER INTO THREE TIERS AND REVISE THEM AT DIFFERENT RATES. Tier A (about 35 rows): national posts that are always askable — CJI, CEC and Election Commissioners, CAG, Attorney General, Cabinet Secretary, Foreign Secretary, RBI Governor and Deputy Governors, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, NABARD, SIDBI, NHB, EXIM, the three service chiefs and the Chief of Defence Staff, NITI Aayog Vice-Chairman, ISRO and DRDO chiefs, chairs of LIC and the large public sector banks, Lok Sabha Speaker, Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman. Revise weekly. Tier B (about 20 rows): heads of international organisations and Indians appointed to international posts. Revise fortnightly. Tier C: brand ambassadors, sports body heads, newly constituted committee chairs. Revise monthly and accept that this tier is lossy.

4. STORE THE ORDINAL. 'Surya Kant is the 53rd Chief Justice of India, sworn in on 24 November 2025, in office until 9 February 2027, succeeding B. R. Gavai.' The ordinal is a distinct field that the exam asks about directly, and it is free to store once you are already writing the row. Two ordinals worth locking now because they collide: the current RBI Governor is the 26th holder of that office, and the current Chief Election Commissioner is the 26th holder of his. Same number, different posts — write both down together so the collision is neutralised rather than discovered in the exam.

5. BUILD LIST ONE: TENURES FIXED BY LAW. These do not change and are worth memorising outright. Comptroller and Auditor General — 6 years or age 65, whichever is earlier (Article 148). Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners — 6 years or age 65, whichever is earlier (CEC and Other ECs Act, 2023). UPSC Chairman and Members — 6 years or age 65 (Article 316). Supreme Court judge — retires at 65 (Article 124); High Court judge — retires at 62 (Article 217). Central Vigilance Commissioner and Vigilance Commissioners — 4 years or age 65. Lokpal Chairperson and Members — 5 years or age 70. NHRC Chairperson and Members — 3 years or age 70 (Protection of Human Rights Act as amended in 2019). Note the CJI has no separate term at all: a CJI serves until the day he turns 65, which is why the end date is a specific calendar date, not a round number of years.

6. BUILD LIST TWO, KEPT PHYSICALLY SEPARATE: TERMS SET BY THE APPOINTMENT ORDER, NOT BY STATUTE. This is where aspirants lose marks by importing a practice into a law. The RBI Governor is the headline case. Section 8 of the RBI Act, 1934 provides that the Governor and up to four Deputy Governors are appointed by the Central Government and hold office for a term NOT EXCEEDING five years, as fixed by the Government at the time of appointment, and are eligible for re-appointment. The Act therefore sets a ceiling, not a term. The current Governor, Sanjay Malhotra, the 26th holder of the office, was appointed for three years from 11 December 2024 — three years is what this appointment order said, not what the statute says. If a question asks 'the maximum term of the RBI Governor under the RBI Act', the answer is five years; if it asks the term of the present incumbent's appointment, it is three. Also in this list: SEBI Chairman (term specified in the appointment order), Cabinet Secretary (initial two-year term, extendable), and the service chiefs (until age 62 or three years in the post, whichever is earlier).

7. RUN A FIXED WEEKLY MAINTENANCE LOOP. One 30-minute slot a week, same day every week: read the week's appointments from a monthly current-affairs PDF, add rows in the standard format, delete rows that have fallen out of the six-month window, and re-read the previous four weeks of additions. Adding without pruning is how the register becomes unusable by November.

8. DRILL BY COVERING COLUMNS, NOT BY READING. Cover the Name column and recover it from the Post; then cover Post and recover from Name; then cover Predecessor. Three passes over 35 rows takes about six minutes. Reading the register end to end feels like revision and does not produce recall under a 20-minute sectional clock.

9. TRIAGE ON EXAM DAY. GA is 40 questions in 20 minutes — 30 seconds each. An appointment question you know resolves in 8 seconds. If you are hesitating past 15 seconds, you do not have the row; leave it blank rather than pick between two names, because a wrong attempt costs 0.25 against a blank and 1.25 against a correct answer.
tricks: Store the predecessor in every row. Roughly a third of appointment questions are phrased as 'X succeeded whom' or 'Y was succeeded by', and the predecessor field answers both directions from a single stored fact. It also gives you an independent cross-check when two names feel equally familiar.

Revise by month-of-appointment rather than by post type. Human memory for a churning list is far better organised by when the news happened than by category, and the exam's own six-month window is a time window, so the retrieval cue you rehearse matches the cue the question supplies.

Keep the two tenure lists on physically separate sheets, in different-coloured ink. The single most common wrong answer in this topic is quoting an administrative practice as a statutory term. Physical separation is a cheap structural fix that a mental note is not.

Write the end date, not just the start date, for posts with a known expiry — the CJI's retirement date, a Governor's appointment end. It converts a two-fact question ('when appointed' and 'until when') into one line, and it tells you at a glance which rows are about to churn before the exam.

Neutralise ordinal collisions deliberately. When two posts share an ordinal number, write both on the same line the first time you notice it. Collisions discovered under exam pressure cost 20 seconds and often a mark; collisions pre-loaded cost nothing.
traps: 'Appointed on' versus 'took charge on' versus 'sworn in on'. These are three different dates for the same person and all three appear as options. Justice Surya Kant was recommended and notified as the next CJI in late October 2025 but took oath on 24 November 2025. Read which of the three verbs the stem uses before choosing.

Statutory tenure imported from administrative practice. The RBI Governor is the recurring casualty: the RBI Act says the term shall not exceed five years, while recent appointment orders have specified three. A question about the Act wants five; a question about the incumbent's order wants three. Answering 'three years as per the RBI Act' is wrong even though three years is the incumbent's actual term.

Acting or interim holders treated as regular. Between a retirement and a fresh appointment, a post may be held in an acting capacity. Questions dated inside that gap have a different correct answer from questions dated after, and the register row must carry the qualifier 'acting' or it will mislead you.

Elected versus appointed, and nominated versus elected. Heads of international bodies reach office by different mechanisms — some elected by a membership vote, some appointed by a board, some nominated by a member state and confirmed. A stem asking 'who was elected' excludes anyone who was appointed, and that single word changes which of the five options is correct.

Chairman versus Managing Director and CEO. In banks and financial institutions these are frequently two different people, and after the separation of the roles in several public sector banks the two names differ. An option pairing the right institution with the right person but the wrong designation is still wrong.

Ordinal drift. 'The 26th Governor of the RBI' and 'the 26th Chief Election Commissioner' are two different people who happen to share a number. Options exploit this by offering the right ordinal attached to the wrong office.
ga-appointments.timeTarget: 8–12 seconds for a row you hold; abandon at 15 seconds. Across a 40-question, 20-minute GA section, appointment questions are the ones that should buy time for the harder banking and scheme questions, not consume it.
ga-appointments.masteryCheck: Cover the Name column of your Tier A register (about 35 rows) and recover every name from the post alone in under four minutes with at most two misses. Then, separately and from memory, write the seven statutory tenures (CAG, CEC/ECs, UPSC, SC judge, HC judge, CVC, NHRC, Lokpal) with both the year figure and the age cap, and beneath a ruled line write the four posts whose terms come from the appointment order rather than statute, including the RBI Governor with BOTH numbers: five years as the statutory ceiling under Section 8, three years as the current incumbent's appointment. You own the topic when you clear both halves on three consecutive weekly attempts — and mastery here expires, so a pass in September does not carry to December without the weekly loop.
questionPatterns: Succession: 'Justice Surya Kant, who took oath as the 53rd Chief Justice of India, succeeded — (a) D. Y. Chandrachud (b) Sanjiv Khanna (c) B. R. Gavai (d) U. U. Lalit (e) N. V. Ramana'. Answer (c).

Statutory tenure: 'Under the RBI Act, 1934, the Governor of the Reserve Bank of India holds office for a term — (a) of exactly 3 years (b) of exactly 5 years (c) not exceeding 5 years, as fixed by the Central Government (d) not exceeding 6 years or until age 65 (e) at the pleasure of the President with no statutory limit'. Answer (c). The same paper may separately ask the incumbent's actual appointment term, which is three years from 11 December 2024.
Ordinal: 'Sanjay Malhotra is the ___ Governor of the Reserve Bank of India. (a) 24th (b) 25th (c) 26th (d) 27th (e) 28th'. Answer (c).

Post-holder match: 'Who currently heads the Securities and Exchange Board of India? (a) Madhabi Puri Buch (b) Tuhin Kanta Pandey (c) Ajay Tyagi (d) G. Mahalingam (e) Ananth Narayan G.' Answer (b), the 11th SEBI Chairman — re-verify before the exam, as this is a churning row.

Constitutional tenure: 'The Comptroller and Auditor General of India holds office for — (a) 5 years or age 62 (b) 6 years or age 65, whichever is earlier (c) 6 years only (d) until age 62 (e) 4 years or age 65'. Answer (b), under Article 148.

Two-part match: a five-row match-the-following pairing organisations (IMF, World Bank, WTO, WHO, ADB) with their current heads, with five permutation options (a)–(e). This is the standard international-appointments format and is why the Tier B register needs its own fortnightly pass.
