ga-negotiable.weightageNote: Zero questions in Prelims — GA is a Mains-only section (40 questions, 50 marks, 20 minutes). The app's ~11Q Mains figure describes the whole banking-awareness cluster this topic belongs to, not 11 questions on negotiable instruments alone. In recent Mains papers current affairs dominate GA, with banking-static heads such as this one appearing as a handful of questions; the payoff is that the content is finite and does not change year to year, so it is cheap to hold.

ga-npa.topicName: NPA, SARFAESI, IBC and Basel Norms
ga-npa.whatItIs: This is the bad-loan and bank-capital cluster. An NPA is a loan where interest or principal is overdue beyond 90 days. SARFAESI (2002) lets a secured creditor seize and sell security without going to court. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016) is the time-bound resolution route for corporate defaults through NCLT. Basel norms are the international capital-adequacy standards set by the Basel Committee, which RBI applies to Indian banks at ratios stricter than the global minimum. For IBPS Clerk Mains these appear as definition, threshold, timeline and percentage questions.
ga-npa.coreMethod:
1. Fix the NPA definition and its sub-classification as a ladder. NPA = interest/principal overdue more than 90 days on a term loan, an out-of-order cash credit/overdraft for 90 days, or bills overdue 90 days. For agriculture the test is crop seasons: two crop seasons for short-duration crops, one crop season for long-duration crops.
2. Learn the pre-NPA warning stage separately: Special Mention Accounts. SMA-0 = overdue 1-30 days, SMA-1 = 31-60 days, SMA-2 = 61-90 days. Beyond 90 it stops being SMA and becomes an NPA. Worked example: 'An account is 45 days overdue. It is classified as — (a) SMA-0 (b) SMA-1 (c) SMA-2 (d) Sub-standard (e) Doubtful.' 45 falls in the 31-60 band, so the answer is (b).
3. Then the NPA sub-classes by age: Sub-standard = NPA for up to 12 months; Doubtful = has stayed sub-standard beyond 12 months (D1 up to 1 year, D2 one to three years, D3 beyond three years); Loss asset = loss identified by the bank, its auditors or RBI but not yet written off. Attach the provisioning percentages: sub-standard 15% (secured) and 25% (unsecured), D1 25%, D2 40%, D3 100%, loss asset 100%.
4. SARFAESI in five facts: full name Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002; applies where the secured debt is ₹1 lakh or more and the outstanding is at least 20% of principal plus interest; Section 13(2) gives the borrower a 60-day notice; Section 13(4) allows possession, management or sale of the secured asset; Section 17 lets the borrower apply to the Debts Recovery Tribunal within 45 days. It does not apply to unsecured loans or to agricultural land. Asset Reconstruction Companies register with RBI; CERSAI is the central registry of security interests.
5. IBC in five facts: enacted 2016; regulator is the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI), which came into existence on 1 October 2016; the adjudicating authority is NCLT for companies and LLPs, DRT for individuals and partnership firms; the minimum default threshold for initiating corporate insolvency was raised to ₹1 crore on 24 March 2020; the corporate insolvency resolution process runs 180 days, extendable by 90 days, with an outer limit of 330 days including litigation time. A Committee of Creditors of financial creditors approves a resolution plan with a 66% vote. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Bill, 2025 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 12 August 2025 and referred to a Select Committee — check its current status close to your exam rather than assuming it has become law.
6. Basel in a fixed sequence: the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision sits at the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, Switzerland. Basel I (1988) covered credit risk with an 8% minimum. Basel II (2004) introduced the three pillars — minimum capital requirement, supervisory review, market discipline. Basel III (2010) followed the global financial crisis and RBI began implementing it from 1 April 2013. India's numbers are stricter than the global ones: minimum CRAR 9% against Basel's 8%, minimum CET1 5.5% against Basel's 4.5%, Tier 1 7%, capital conservation buffer 2.5%, so total requirement with buffer is 11.5% and CET1 with buffer is 8%. Leverage ratio 4% for domestic systemically important banks and 3.5% for other banks. LCR and NSFR both 100%.
7. Add the forward-looking item: RBI's Expected Credit Loss provisioning framework and the revised Basel III capital norms are set to apply from 1 April 2027, with a glide path to 31 March 2031. Under ECL, assets sit in Stage 1, 2 or 3 rather than the current incurred-loss buckets.
8. In the exam, identify which of the four sub-areas the question is in from its first six words, then reach for that sub-area's number list. Do not attempt to reason a percentage out — either it is memorised or you skip.
tricks: Store the four Basel-India numbers as a single ascending run: 5.5 - 7 - 9 - 11.5 (CET1, Tier 1, CRAR, CRAR with buffer). Recalling one anchors the rest, and the 2.5% conservation buffer is simply the gap between 9 and 11.5.

Remember 90 as the pivot: below 90 days the account is SMA, at and beyond 90 days it is an NPA. The SMA bands are then just the 90 split into three thirties, which removes any need to memorise the three ranges separately.

Doubtful-asset provisioning steps 25-40-100 for D1-D2-D3, which is easy to hold as 'quarter, then not-quite-half, then all'. Sub-standard sits below at 15% secured and 25% unsecured — note the unsecured sub-standard figure equals the D1 figure, so you only carry one extra number.

SARFAESI's two clocks are 60 and 45: sixty days for the borrower to pay after the 13(2) notice, forty-five days to appeal to the DRT under Section 17. Any option offering ninety days for either is a distractor imported from the NPA rule.

IBC's timeline is 180 + 90 = 270 for the process itself, with 330 as the outer wall because it additionally absorbs litigation time. If a five-option question offers both 270 and 330, read whether the stem says 'including time taken in legal proceedings' — that phrase selects 330.
traps: SMA-0 is 1-30 days overdue, not zero days overdue. The '0' names the band, not the day count, and papers exploit that by offering 'no overdue' as a distractor.

The SARFAESI trigger is a secured debt of ₹1 lakh or more; the IBC corporate-insolvency default threshold is ₹1 crore. These two figures get swapped in options constantly, and they belong to different statutes with different forums (DRT versus NCLT).

SARFAESI cannot be used against agricultural land, and it does not apply to unsecured lending at all. A question describing an unsecured personal loan gone bad and asking whether the bank can enforce security under SARFAESI is answered 'no', not 'yes after 60 days'.

India's minimum CRAR is 9%, not the Basel global figure of 8%, and CET1 is 5.5%, not 4.5%. Options carrying the international numbers are placed there precisely for candidates who memorised the Basel text instead of the RBI application.

The Capital Conservation Buffer (2.5%) and the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (a 0-2.5% range) are different things. The conservation buffer is a standing requirement; the countercyclical buffer is switched on when credit growth overheats and has not been activated in India.

Under RBI's clarification, an NPA can be upgraded to standard only after the entire arrears of interest and principal are repaid — not after a part-payment that brings the overdue below 90 days. Options suggesting partial payment restores standard status are wrong.
ga-npa.timeTarget: Aim for 12-18 seconds per question in Mains, since these are recall items. Longer statement-combination questions on Basel or IBC may take 25 seconds, and if the specific percentage does not surface within that window, skip rather than guess at 0.25 negative. Learning target: two 50-minute blocks to build the number sheets, then 10 minutes weekly.
ga-npa.masteryCheck: On a blank sheet in 3 minutes, reproduce: the 90-day rule plus the three SMA bands; the four NPA classes with their provisioning percentages; SARFAESI's ₹1 lakh threshold, 60-day notice and 45-day DRT appeal; IBC's ₹1 crore threshold, 180+90 and 330-day limits, NCLT/DRT split and 66% CoC vote; and the India-specific Basel run 5.5 / 7 / 9 / 11.5 with the 2.5% conservation buffer. Then take 12 five-option MCQs spanning all four sub-areas in under 4 minutes with at most two wrong.
questionPatterns: Single-number recall against five numeric options — 'Under Basel III as implemented by RBI, the minimum Common Equity Tier 1 ratio for Indian banks is (a) 4.5% (b) 5.5% (c) 6% (d) 7% (e) 8%' — answer (b), because India applies a stricter figure than the Basel global 4.5%.

Classification scenario — an account with a stated number of overdue days or a stated period as an NPA, asked to be placed into SMA-0/1/2, sub-standard, doubtful or loss, with the five categories as the five options.

Statute-matching — 'The 60-day notice to a defaulting borrower before enforcement of security is issued under which Act/section?' with SARFAESI Section 13(2) among five statutory choices; or a match-the-following between SARFAESI, IBC, RDDBFI and Basel and their years/forums.

Statement-combination on IBC — three statements about the adjudicating authority, the default threshold and the resolution timeline, with five combination options including 'All of these' and 'None of these'.
Current-affairs overlay — the date from which RBI's Expected Credit Loss framework applies, or the status of the IBC (Amendment) Bill, 2025, presented against five dates or five status descriptions.
ga-npa.searchQuery: RBI NPA classification SMA 90 days provisioning norms SARFAESI section 13(2) IBC 330 days threshold Basel III India CRAR 9 percent CET1 5.5 expected credit loss April 2027
ga-npa.aiPrompt: Act as an IBPS Clerk Mains General Awareness question setter. Produce 18 multiple-choice questions covering four areas in equal measure: (1) NPA definition, SMA sub-classification and provisioning norms, (2) the SARFAESI Act 2002, (3) the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016, and (4) Basel norms as implemented by RBI in India. EVERY question must have EXACTLY FIVE options labelled (a) to (e) — the IBPS pattern is five options, never four. Use the India-specific Basel figures (CRAR 9%, CET1 5.5%, Tier 1 7%, capital conservation buffer 2.5%) as correct answers and place the international Basel figures among the distractors. Include at least four statement-combination questions whose five options are combinations like 'Only I and II', 'Only II and III', 'All of these', 'None of these'. Provide an answer key with a one-line justification for each, naming the relevant section, circular or ratio. Do not ask anything whose answer changed after 2025 unless you state the effective date inside the question.
ga-npa.blockPlan: This needs two 50-minute GA blocks because of the number density. Block A (50 min): NPA and SARFAESI — build one sheet with the 90-day pivot, SMA bands, four NPA classes with provisioning, and the SARFAESI 1 lakh / 60 / 45 trio. Block B (50 min, next day): IBC and Basel — the NCLT/DRT split, 1 crore / 180+90 / 330 / 66%, then the Basel run 5.5-7-9-11.5 plus LCR, NSFR and the April 2027 ECL date. Revision touches of 10 minutes at day 4, day 10 and day 25, each time reproducing the number sheets from memory before looking. Keep these in the tail-end GA slot of your 4-hour day.
ga-npa.websiteRef: rbi.org.in — Master Circular on Prudential Norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning, and the Master Circular on Basel III Capital Regulations; ibbi.gov.in for IBC timelines and thresholds
ga-npa.weightageNote: Nil in Prelims; GA is Mains-only at 40 questions and 50 marks in 20 minutes. The ~11Q Mains estimate covers the banking-awareness cluster as a whole rather than this topic by itself. This head is number-heavy, so it rewards a written number sheet more than reading, and the same numbers recur across SBI, IBPS and RRB papers, making the effort transferable.

ga-moneymarket.topicName: Money Market — T-bills, Commercial Paper, CDs, Call Money
ga-moneymarket.whatItIs: The money market is the market for funds and instruments of less than one year, regulated by RBI. Its purpose is short-term liquidity management for banks, corporates and the government. The instruments to know are call, notice and term money; Treasury bills and Cash Management Bills issued by the government; Commercial Paper issued by corporates and NBFCs; Certificates of Deposit issued by banks; and the collateralised segment, chiefly TREPS and repo. Around this sits RBI's policy corridor — repo, SDF, MSF and the Bank Rate — which Mains tests almost every year.
ga-moneymarket.coreMethod:
1. Sort every instrument on two axes only: who issues it, and how long it runs. That pair answers most questions. Government issues T-bills and CMBs; banks issue CDs; corporates and NBFCs issue CP; banks and primary dealers deal in call/notice/term money.
2. Fix the maturity ladder in ascending order and rehearse it as one line: call money = overnight (one day); notice money = 2 to 14 days; term money = 15 days to one year; CP = 7 days to one year; CD = 7 days to one year; T-bills = 91, 182 and 364 days; CMBs = less than 91 days.
3. Fix the size ladder next: T-bills and CMBs come in a minimum of ₹10,000 and multiples of ₹10,000; CP and CD both carry a minimum denomination of ₹5 lakh and multiples of ₹5 lakh. Two numbers, ten thousand and five lakh, cover the whole size family.
4. Learn the discount principle once and apply it everywhere: T-bills, CMBs, CP and CDs are all issued at a discount to face value and redeemed at face value. There is no coupon; the investor's return is the discount. Worked example: 'Which of the following is issued at a discount to face value and carries no periodic interest? (a) 10-year government security (b) 91-day Treasury bill (c) Equity share (d) Non-convertible debenture (e) Preference share' — answer (b), because T-bills are zero-coupon discount instruments while a G-sec pays a half-yearly coupon.
5. Attach the auction and form facts: T-bills are auctioned by RBI on behalf of the government, 91-day weekly and 182-day and 364-day on alternate weeks; CP and NCDs of up to one-year maturity are governed by RBI's Commercial Paper and Non-Convertible Debentures Directions, 2024, in force from 1 April 2024, and must be in dematerialised form with a SEBI-registered depository. CDs are governed by RBI's Certificate of Deposit Directions, 2021.
6. Learn the collateralised segment: TREPS (Triparty Repo) was introduced in 2018 through the Clearing Corporation of India and replaced CBLO. Repo is a sale with an agreement to repurchase; reverse repo is the mirror.
7. Layer the policy corridor on top, with current values: repo rate 5.25%, SDF 5.00% as the floor, MSF and Bank Rate at the ceiling 25 basis points above repo, CRR 3.00% after the phased reduction completed on 29 November 2025, SLR 18.00%. The Standing Deposit Facility replaced the fixed reverse repo as the floor of the corridor in April 2022 and, unlike reverse repo, is uncollateralised. Verify the repo rate against the latest MPC outcome before your exam, because it is the single most frequently updated number in this topic.
8. In the exam, decide first whether the question is about an instrument or about a policy rate. Instrument questions are answered from the maturity/size/issuer ladders; policy-rate questions are answered from the current corridor. Mixing the two is where candidates lose the mark.
tricks: Compress the whole maturity ladder into 'one, two-to-fourteen, fifteen-to-a-year, then seven-to-a-year for the paper instruments, then 91-182-364'. Reciting it in that order gives you the answer to any 'minimum/maximum tenor' question in under ten seconds without reasoning.

Only two minimum-denomination numbers exist in this topic: ₹10,000 for government bills and ₹5 lakh for CP and CD. If a five-option question offers ₹1 lakh, ₹25 lakh or ₹1 crore, those are automatically distractors, which usually leaves you choosing between two.

Every short-term paper here is a discount instrument, so any option that describes a T-bill, CP or CD as paying a coupon or a fixed quarterly interest can be dropped on sight — this alone removes one or two of the five.

Hold the corridor as a three-number sandwich around repo: SDF = repo minus 25 bps, MSF = Bank Rate = repo plus 25 bps. Learn only the repo rate as a live figure and derive the other three, so a mid-year MPC change forces you to update one number rather than four.

When a question names a participant, use it as the filter: only banks issue CDs, only corporates/NBFCs/all-India financial institutions issue CP, only the government issues T-bills. A stem beginning 'A manufacturing company raises short-term funds by issuing…' has already told you the answer is Commercial Paper.
traps: Call money is overnight, not 'up to 14 days'. The 2-to-14-day band belongs to notice money, and term money starts at 15 days. Papers rotate these three bands among the options deliberately.

T-bills are issued in three tenors only — 91, 182 and 364 days. There is no 30-day, 90-day or 270-day Treasury bill in India, and the 364-day bill is not a '360-day' or 'one-year' bill; the exact figure 364 is what is tested.

CMBs are not T-bills with a different name: they are issued for maturities of less than 91 days to bridge temporary cash mismatches, and their tenor is flexible rather than one of the three standard buckets.

The SDF replaced the fixed-rate reverse repo as the corridor floor in April 2022 and is uncollateralised, whereas reverse repo involves government securities as collateral. Options describing SDF as collateralised, or describing reverse repo as the current floor, are wrong.

CRR is now 3.00% following the four 25-basis-point tranches completed on 29 November 2025. Answering 4% from older study material is the most likely single error on this topic, and SLR at 18.00% has been unchanged since April 2020 — do not assume it moved with CRR.
CP has a minimum tenor of seven days and a maximum of one year. The old idea that CP starts at 15 days is out of date under the 2024 Directions.
ga-moneymarket.timeTarget: 10-15 seconds per instrument question and 8-10 seconds per policy-rate question in Mains, since both are direct recall. Allow 25 seconds only for statement-combination questions. Learning target: one 45-minute block for the ladders plus a 5-minute check of the current repo rate every time RBI announces a policy (six bi-monthly meetings a year).
ga-moneymarket.masteryCheck: In 2 minutes write out: the maturity band for call, notice and term money; the three T-bill tenors and the CMB rule; minimum denominations for T-bills, CP and CD; who may issue each of CP, CD and T-bills; the fact that all of these are discount instruments; and the current repo, SDF, MSF/Bank Rate, CRR and SLR. Then answer 10 five-option MCQs in 2 minutes with at most one wrong. If you cannot state today's repo rate without hesitating, you have not finished this topic.
questionPatterns: Tenor recall — 'The minimum and maximum tenor of Commercial Paper is (a) 7 days to 1 year (b) 15 days to 1 year (c) 1 day to 90 days (d) 91 days to 364 days (e) 7 days to 3 years' — answer (a) under the RBI Directions of 2024.
Issuer identification from a scenario — a company, a bank or the government raising short-term funds, with the five instruments as options; solved by the issuer filter rather than by any calculation.

Policy-corridor recall — the current repo rate, the SDF rate, the Bank Rate, CRR or SLR, offered as five numeric choices; occasionally framed as 'the floor of the LAF corridor is' with SDF, reverse repo, MSF, Bank Rate and repo as the five options.

Statement-combination on money-market features — three statements on discount pricing, denomination and dematerialised form, with five combination options including 'All of these' and 'None of these'.
Match-the-following between instruments and tenors/issuers, presented as five permutation options; the ladder recited in order resolves it directly.
ga-moneymarket.searchQuery: RBI money market instruments call notice term money treasury bills 91 182 364 minimum 10000 commercial paper certificate of deposit 5 lakh directions 2024 2021 TREPS repo SDF current rates
ga-moneymarket.aiPrompt: Act as an IBPS Clerk Mains General Awareness question setter. Write 15 multiple-choice questions on the Indian money market: call/notice/term money, Treasury bills, Cash Management Bills, Commercial Paper, Certificates of Deposit, TREPS and repo, plus RBI's policy corridor (repo, SDF, MSF, Bank Rate, CRR, SLR). EVERY question must have EXACTLY FIVE options labelled (a) to (e); IBPS never uses five options. Base tenor and denomination answers on the RBI (Commercial Paper and Non-Convertible Debentures) Directions, 2024 and the RBI (Certificate of Deposit) Directions, 2021 — that is, CP and CD tenor 7 days to 1 year and minimum denomination ₹5 lakh, T-bills at 91/182/364 days with a ₹10,000 minimum. For any policy-rate question, state the effective date inside the question stem so it does not go stale. Include 4 statement-combination questions with five combination options and 2 questions whose answer is 'None of these'. Give an answer key with a one-line reason for each.
ga-moneymarket.blockPlan: One 45-minute GA block plus a standing 5-minute policy check. Block A (45 min): write the maturity ladder, the size ladder and the issuer filter as three short lists, then the corridor sandwich (SDF = repo − 25 bps, MSF = Bank Rate = repo + 25 bps) with today's values. Revision 1 (10 min, day 4): reproduce all three lists blind, then 12 five-option MCQs. Revision 2 (10 min, day 15): corridor values only, plus TREPS/CBLO and the 2024 CP Directions. Additionally, after every RBI bi-monthly policy announcement, spend 5 minutes updating the repo rate and re-deriving SDF, MSF and Bank Rate. Place this in the end-of-day GA slot.
ga-moneymarket.websiteRef: rbi.org.in — Master Direction on Commercial Paper and Non-Convertible Debentures (2024), Certificate of Deposit Directions (2021), and the current policy rates panel on the RBI home page
ga-moneymarket.weightageNote: Nil in Prelims; GA appears only in Mains at 40 questions and 50 marks in 20 minutes. The ~11Q Mains figure describes the banking-awareness cluster this topic sits inside. Policy-rate questions from this topic are among the most predictable GA items because RBI announces them on a fixed bi-monthly calendar, but they are also the fastest to go stale, so the maintenance cost is real.

ga-capitalmarket.topicName: Capital Market — Shares, Bonds, Debentures, Mutual Funds
ga-capitalmarket.whatItIs: The capital market handles funds of more than one year and is regulated by SEBI. It splits into the primary market, where securities are issued for the first time (IPO, FPO, rights and private placement), and the secondary market, where they trade on exchanges. The instruments to know are equity and preference shares, debentures and bonds, and pooled vehicles — mutual funds and the newer Specialised Investment Funds. For IBPS Clerk Mains, the questions are about who regulates what, ownership versus creditorship, instrument definitions, and recent SEBI changes.
ga-capitalmarket.coreMethod:
1. Draw the ownership-versus-creditorship line first, because it decides a large share of the questions. An equity share makes you an owner: voting rights, variable dividend, paid last in liquidation. A debenture or bond makes you a creditor: no voting rights, fixed interest payable whether or not there is profit, paid before shareholders. Preference shares sit between — fixed dividend, priority over equity in dividend and repayment, normally no voting rights.
2. Worked example: 'Which of the following instrument holders are creditors of the company rather than owners? (a) Equity shareholders (b) Preference shareholders (c) Debenture holders (d) Promoters (e) Both (a) and (b)' — answer (c), because interest on debentures is a charge on profit and is payable regardless of profitability, whereas share dividends are an appropriation of profit.
3. Learn the preference-share sub-types as pairs: cumulative versus non-cumulative (does unpaid dividend accumulate?), participating versus non-participating (does it share surplus profit?), convertible versus non-convertible, redeemable versus irredeemable. Under the Companies Act, 2013 preference shares must be redeemable, with a maximum tenure of twenty years.
4. Learn debenture sub-types the same way: secured versus unsecured, convertible (fully or partly) versus non-convertible, and registered versus bearer.
5. Fix the SEBI facts: SEBI was set up in 1988 and given statutory status by the SEBI Act, 1992; its headquarters is in Mumbai; the current chairman is Tuhin Kanta Pandey, who took charge on 1 March 2025 for a three-year term. SEBI regulates the securities market, including mutual funds; RBI regulates the money market and government securities.
6. Fix the mutual-fund facts: governed by the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996; the structure is a three-tier sponsor, trustee and asset management company; the price is the Net Asset Value; open-ended funds can be bought and redeemed continuously while close-ended funds have a fixed maturity and trade on an exchange; ELSS carries a three-year lock-in, the shortest among tax-saving instruments; AMFI is the industry association. The first mutual fund in India was UTI, set up in 1963. SEBI's risk-o-meter classifies schemes on a six-level scale.
7. Add the recent layer, which Mains favours: Indian equity settlement moved to T+1 in January 2024, with an optional same-day T+0 beta introduced from 28 March 2024. SEBI operationalised Specialised Investment Funds as a new product category between mutual funds and portfolio management services from 1 April 2025, with a minimum investment of ₹10 lakh across strategies. Depositories are NSDL and CDSL; exchanges of note are BSE (established 1875, Asia's oldest) and NSE, with Sensex tracking 30 stocks and Nifty 50 tracking fifty.
8. In the exam, classify the question in two seconds — instrument, regulator, or recent reform — then draw from that shelf. Do not try to derive; capital-market GA is definition recall.
tricks: Anchor everything to one sentence: 'shareholders own, debenture holders lend'. Every dividend-versus-interest, voting-versus-no-voting and priority-in-liquidation question falls out of it, which is typically three of the five options gone at once.

Use the regulator split as a first filter — SEBI for anything traded on an exchange or pooled into a fund, RBI for anything under one year or government-debt related, IRDAI for insurance, PFRDA for pension. A question naming the instrument tells you the regulator without any further recall.

Preference shares are the 'both' instrument: fixed return like debt, but still share capital. When a five-option question asks which instrument has features of both equity and debt, the answer is preference share unless a convertible debenture is explicitly offered.

Remember three dates as a run: 1988 SEBI set up, 1992 statutory, 1996 mutual fund regulations. A single ascending sequence is cheaper to hold than three isolated facts and covers a common date question.
For settlement-cycle questions, hold 'T+1 is the standard, T+0 is optional'. Options that describe T+0 as compulsory or T+2 as current are then rejected immediately.
traps: Debenture holders receive interest, not dividend, and they receive it whether or not the company makes a profit. Any option describing debenture returns as 'dividend depending on profit' is wrong even when the numbers look right.
SEBI was established in 1988 but became a statutory body in 1992. Questions phrase this precisely — 'established' versus 'given statutory powers' — and both years appear among the five options.

Irredeemable preference shares cannot be issued under the Companies Act, 2013; the maximum redemption period is twenty years. Options offering perpetual or irredeemable preference shares as a valid Indian instrument are distractors.
Mutual funds are regulated by SEBI, not by RBI, even when the fund is sponsored by a bank. The sponsor's identity does not change the regulator.
T+0 settlement is available on an optional beta basis alongside T+1 — it is not the market-wide default. Treating T+0 as the mandatory Indian settlement cycle is a common error.

Specialised Investment Funds have a ₹10 lakh minimum investment and are a distinct SEBI category — not a mutual fund scheme with a large ticket size, and not a portfolio management service. The ₹10 lakh figure is the tested detail.
ga-capitalmarket.timeTarget: 12-15 seconds for a definition or regulator question, up to 25 seconds for statement-combination or match-the-following. Learning target: one 45-minute block for instruments plus one 30-minute block for SEBI and mutual funds, then 10 minutes of revision a fortnight.
ga-capitalmarket.masteryCheck: In 2 minutes write: three differences between an equity share and a debenture; the four preference-share pairs plus the twenty-year redemption cap; SEBI's 1988/1992/Mumbai/current-chairman facts; the three-tier mutual fund structure, the 1996 Regulations, NAV, open versus close-ended and the ELSS lock-in; and the current settlement cycle plus the SIF minimum. Then take 10 five-option MCQs in 2 minutes, at most one wrong.
questionPatterns: Ownership-versus-creditor identification — 'Holders of which of the following are creditors of the company?' with equity shares, preference shares, debentures, bonus shares and rights shares as the five options.

Regulator matching — 'Mutual funds in India are regulated by (a) RBI (b) SEBI (c) IRDAI (d) PFRDA (e) AMFI' — answer (b); AMFI is placed as the trap because it is an industry association, not a regulator.

Date and institution recall — the year SEBI became statutory, the year of the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, the oldest stock exchange in Asia, or the current SEBI chairman, each against five choices.
Statement-combination on mutual funds — three statements about NAV, open-ended schemes and ELSS lock-in, with five combination options such as 'Only I and III', 'All of these', 'None of these'.
Recent-reform recall — the current settlement cycle, the launch of Specialised Investment Funds or their minimum investment amount, presented as five numeric or descriptive choices.
ga-capitalmarket.searchQuery: SEBI Act 1992 statutory 1988 mutual funds regulations 1996 equity preference shares debentures difference T+1 T+0 settlement specialised investment fund 10 lakh SEBI chairman
ga-capitalmarket.aiPrompt: Act as an IBPS Clerk Mains General Awareness question setter. Create 15 multiple-choice questions on the Indian capital market covering: primary versus secondary market, equity and preference shares, debentures and bonds, mutual funds (structure, NAV, open/close-ended, ELSS), SEBI as regulator, and recent reforms (T+1 settlement with optional T+0, Specialised Investment Funds with a ₹10 lakh minimum). EVERY question must have EXACTLY FIVE options labelled (a) to (e) — the IBPS pattern is five options, not four. Include at least three questions that test the ownership-versus-creditorship distinction, three date/institution recall questions, and four statement-combination questions whose five options are combinations such as 'Only II', 'Only I and III', 'All of these', 'None of these'. Where a fact could change, state the effective date inside the stem. Supply an answer key with a one-line reason for each question, and do not include any question that depends on current share prices or index levels.
ga-capitalmarket.blockPlan: Two blocks totalling 75 minutes. Block A (45 min): instruments — draw a three-column table for equity share, preference share and debenture across ownership, return type, voting, priority in liquidation and tenure, then add the four preference-share pairs and the debenture sub-types. Block B (30 min, next day): SEBI facts, the three-tier mutual fund structure, the 1988/1992/1996 date run, and the recent reforms (T+1/T+0, SIF). Revision touches of 10 minutes at day 5 and day 20, reproducing the table blind before checking. Keep both inside the closing GA slot of your 4-hour day rather than displacing Quant or Reasoning practice.
ga-capitalmarket.bookRef: Banking Awareness for SBI & IBPS Bank Clerk/PO/RRB/RBI/LIC Exams, Disha Publication (book only — no chapter verified)
ga-capitalmarket.websiteRef: sebi.gov.in — press releases and the Mutual Funds and Specialised Investment Funds sections; amfiindia.com for mutual fund basics and category definitions
ga-capitalmarket.weightageNote: Nil in Prelims; GA is a Mains-only section of 40 questions and 50 marks in 20 minutes. The ~11Q Mains figure applies to the banking-awareness cluster containing this topic. Capital-market questions in Clerk-level GA stay at the definitional layer — they do not ask for valuation or yield computation — so the content is bounded and mostly stable, apart from the SEBI reform items that need a refresh close to the exam.

ga-inclusion.topicName: Financial Inclusion — PMJDY, PMJJBY, PMSBY, Atal Pension Yojana
ga-inclusion.whatItIs: Four flagship schemes of the Department of Financial Services that together form the government's financial-inclusion and social-security architecture. PMJDY (2014) gives every adult a zero-balance bank account with a RuPay card and overdraft. PMJJBY gives life cover, PMSBY gives accident cover, and Atal Pension Yojana gives a guaranteed pension — the last three are collectively called the Jan Suraksha schemes and were all launched in May 2015. For Mains, everything is numbers: age bands, premiums, cover amounts and launch dates.
ga-inclusion.coreMethod:
1. Build one four-column table — scheme, launch date, age band, benefit and premium. Everything asked about this topic is a cell in that table, so building it once and re-writing it from memory three times is the entire method.
2. PMJDY: launched 28 August 2014; a Basic Savings Bank Deposit Account with zero minimum balance; free RuPay debit card carrying accidental insurance cover of ₹1 lakh for cards issued before 28 August 2018 and ₹2 lakh for cards issued on or after that date; overdraft up to ₹10,000 (of which ₹2,000 without conditions), available to account holders aged 18 to 65; the scheme was extended beyond August 2018 with the focus shifting from 'every household' to 'every unbanked adult'. By 1 July 2026 the scheme had crossed 58 crore accounts with deposits above ₹3.08 lakh crore, and roughly 56% of accounts belong to women and about 78% are in rural and semi-urban areas.
3. PMJJBY: launched 9 May 2015; entry age 18 to 50 years, cover continuing to age 55; ₹2 lakh payable on death from any cause; annual premium ₹436, revised from ₹330 with effect from 1 June 2022; cover year runs 1 June to 31 May with auto-debit from the linked savings account; a lien period applies for non-accidental death in the first weeks of enrolment.
4. PMSBY: launched 9 May 2015; entry age 18 to 70 years; ₹2 lakh for accidental death or total permanent disability and ₹1 lakh for partial permanent disability; annual premium ₹20, revised from ₹12 with effect from 1 June 2022; same 1 June to 31 May cover year and auto-debit mechanism.
5. Atal Pension Yojana: launched 9 May 2015 and administered by PFRDA; entry age 18 to 40 years, so the minimum contribution period is 20 years; guaranteed monthly pension of ₹1,000, ₹2,000, ₹3,000, ₹4,000 or ₹5,000 from age 60; on the subscriber's death the spouse receives the same pension and the nominee receives the accumulated corpus; from 1 October 2022 anyone who is or has been an income-tax payer cannot join, though those enrolled before that date continue.
6. Learn the three-way distinction by cause of death, because that is the standard scenario question: PMJJBY pays on death from any cause; PMSBY pays only on accidental death or disability; both may be held simultaneously, and a person holding both receives from both if death is accidental.
7. Worked example: 'Ravi is 52 years old and has a savings account. Which of the following can he newly enrol in? (a) PMJJBY only (b) PMSBY only (c) Both PMJJBY and PMSBY (d) Atal Pension Yojana only (e) None of these' — PMJJBY entry is capped at 50 and APY at 40, while PMSBY runs to 70, so the answer is (b).
8. Rehearse the table against the calendar: three of the four schemes share 9 May 2015, and only PMJDY is 28 August 2014. That single asymmetry answers most launch-date questions.
tricks: Bind the two premiums to the two covers as a pair of ratios: ₹436 buys ₹2 lakh of any-cause life cover, ₹20 buys ₹2 lakh of accident cover. Both covers are ₹2 lakh, so you only need to remember which premium is large and which is small — the life cover always costs more.

The four age ceilings form a clean ascending run: APY 40, PMJJBY 50, PMJDY overdraft 65, PMSBY 70. Reciting '40-50-65-70' answers every eligibility question in about five seconds without pulling up the whole table.
Three of four schemes launched on 9 May 2015; PMJDY alone is 28 August 2014. For a date question, ask only 'is it PMJDY?' — one binary decision instead of four date recalls.

PMSBY is the accident scheme and both words start with the same sound as 'Suraksha' meaning safety/protection against mishap; PMJJBY is 'Jeevan Jyoti', the life scheme. Fixing this pairing prevents the single most costly confusion on this topic, since the two schemes have identical ₹2 lakh covers and are otherwise easy to swap.

The RuPay accident cover on PMJDY has two values split by one date — ₹1 lakh before 28 August 2018 and ₹2 lakh on or after. If a question gives you a card-issue date, it is testing exactly this split and nothing else.
traps: PMJJBY pays ₹2 lakh on death from any cause, while PMSBY pays ₹2 lakh only for accidental death. Both covers are ₹2 lakh, so the amount does not distinguish them — only the cause does, and questions are built precisely on that overlap.

The APY entry limit is 40, not 45 or 50. Because the pension starts at 60 and a minimum 20 years of contribution is required, 40 is forced by arithmetic — if you see 45 among the options, it contradicts the 20-year rule.

Income-tax payers have been barred from newly joining APY since 1 October 2022, but existing subscribers who joined before that date continue. Options saying all taxpayers were removed from the scheme are wrong.
PMJDY's overdraft is up to ₹10,000, of which ₹2,000 is available without conditions. Papers offer ₹5,000 and ₹2,000 as standalone answers to catch a half-remembered figure.
The current premiums are ₹436 for PMJJBY and ₹20 for PMSBY, revised on 1 June 2022. The older ₹330 and ₹12 figures still circulate in outdated material and are placed among the five options.
APY is regulated by PFRDA, not by RBI or IRDAI, even though enrolment happens at a bank branch. The enrolment channel is not the regulator.
ga-inclusion.timeTarget: 8-12 seconds per question — these are the fastest GA questions in the paper because they are single-cell recall. Allow 20 seconds for a scenario question that requires checking a person's age against two or three schemes. Learning target: one 40-minute block to build the table, then 8 minutes of revision every ten days.
ga-inclusion.masteryCheck: In 90 seconds reproduce the full four-scheme table from blank paper: launch date, age band, benefit amount and annual premium for each, plus the PMJDY overdraft limit and the two RuPay cover values with their cut-off date, plus the APY pension range and the 1 October 2022 taxpayer rule. Then answer 12 five-option MCQs including at least three age-eligibility scenarios in under 2 minutes, with at most one wrong.
questionPatterns: Direct premium or cover recall — 'The annual premium under Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana is (a) ₹12 (b) ₹20 (c) ₹330 (d) ₹436 (e) ₹500' — answer (d), the figure effective from 1 June 2022.

Age-eligibility scenario — a person of a stated age asked which scheme or schemes he may newly join, with five options covering single schemes, combinations and 'None of these'; solved by the 40-50-65-70 run.
Cause-of-benefit discrimination — 'Death due to illness is covered under which scheme?' with PMJJBY, PMSBY, both, either APY or PMSBY, and none as the five options; PMJJBY alone covers any cause.
Statement-combination on PMJDY features — three statements about zero balance, the RuPay cover and the overdraft limit, with five combination options including 'All of these' and 'None of these'.
Regulator/ministry matching — which authority administers APY, or which department runs the Jan Suraksha schemes, against five choices where RBI, IRDAI and PFRDA all appear.

ga-mudra.topicName: MUDRA, Stand-Up India and Startup India
ga-mudra.whatItIs: Three entrepreneurship-credit schemes that Mains treats as one family. Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana (2015) gives collateral-free loans to non-farm micro enterprises through banks, NBFCs and MFIs, refinanced by MUDRA Ltd, a SIDBI subsidiary. Stand-Up India (2016) gives larger loans specifically to Scheduled Caste, Scheduled Tribe and women entrepreneurs setting up a first venture. Startup India (2016) is not a loan scheme at all — it is a DPIIT-run recognition and benefits framework covering tax exemption, self-certification and funding support.
ga-mudra.coreMethod:
1. Separate the three by purpose before touching any number: MUDRA is micro-credit for existing or new small businesses; Stand-Up India is targeted credit for SC/ST and women setting up a greenfield venture; Startup India is recognition plus tax and funding benefits for innovation-driven companies. Confusing these three is the main source of lost marks here.
2. MUDRA numbers, learnt as a four-step ladder: Shishu up to ₹50,000; Kishore above ₹50,000 up to ₹5 lakh; Tarun above ₹5 lakh up to ₹10 lakh; Tarun Plus above ₹10 lakh up to ₹20 lakh. Tarun Plus was announced in the 2024 Budget and made effective from 24 October 2024, and it is available only to borrowers who previously availed and successfully repaid a Tarun-category loan. Loans are collateral-free, the scheme launched on 8 April 2015, and lending is done by scheduled commercial banks, RRBs, small finance banks, NBFCs and MFIs. Cumulatively, more than 59 crore loans worth over ₹41 lakh crore have been sanctioned.
3. Worked example: 'An entrepreneur seeks a ₹7 lakh loan for a micro trading unit under PMMY. The applicable category is (a) Shishu (b) Kishore (c) Tarun (d) Tarun Plus (e) Not covered under PMMY' — ₹7 lakh falls in the above-₹5-lakh-to-₹10-lakh band, so the answer is (c).
4. Stand-Up India numbers: launched 5 April 2016; bank loans between ₹10 lakh and ₹1 crore; at least one Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe borrower and at least one woman borrower per bank branch; the venture must be greenfield, meaning the borrower's first venture, in manufacturing, services, trading or activities allied to agriculture; the loan is composite, covering term loan and working capital; margin money requirement was reduced from up to 25% to up to 15%; repayment up to seven years with a moratorium; the portal is standupmitra.in. Budget 2025-26 announced a new scheme drawing on Stand-Up India's experience, offering term loans up to ₹2 crore to five lakh first-time women, SC and ST entrepreneurs over five years — check its notified name and status before your exam rather than assuming one.
5. Startup India facts: launched 16 January 2016, run by DPIIT under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry; National Startup Day is 16 January; DPIIT recognition requires the entity to be up to ten years old with turnover not exceeding ₹100 crore in any financial year, working on innovation or a scalable business model, and not formed by splitting up or reconstructing an existing business. Benefits include income-tax deduction under Section 80-IAC for any three consecutive years out of ten, with the eligibility window extended to startups incorporated before 1 April 2030; self-certification under labour and environment laws; the Fund of Funds for Startups operated through SIDBI, with Fund of Funds 2.0 of ₹10,000 crore approved by the Cabinet; the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme; and the Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups.
6. In the exam, read the stem for the beneficiary. 'SC/ST or woman' points to Stand-Up India. 'Micro unit, collateral-free, up to ₹20 lakh' points to MUDRA. 'Innovation, DPIIT, tax holiday' points to Startup India. The beneficiary word does most of the work.
tricks: Hold the MUDRA ladder as the number run 50,000 - 5 lakh - 10 lakh - 20 lakh in ascending order and simply place the amount in the question against it. Because the bands are contiguous, no boundary arithmetic is needed and the category falls out in about five seconds.

Stand-Up India's range starts exactly where MUDRA's ends: MUDRA tops out at ₹20 lakh, Stand-Up India runs ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore. Fixing this adjacency means a single loan amount in a stem usually eliminates one of the two schemes immediately.

The three launch dates cluster in one twelve-month window — MUDRA 8 April 2015, Startup India 16 January 2016, Stand-Up India 5 April 2016. Learn them as one timeline in order rather than three isolated dates, which makes 'which was launched first' questions instant.
'Greenfield' is the giveaway word for Stand-Up India and appears in almost every question on it. Seeing it lets you pick the scheme before you have read all five options.

MUDRA Ltd is a subsidiary of SIDBI, and the Fund of Funds for Startups is also operated through SIDBI. Remembering SIDBI as the common institutional thread saves you from mixing in NABARD, which serves rural and agricultural credit instead.
traps: Tarun Plus is not simply 'Tarun with a higher limit' — it is restricted to borrowers who have already taken and fully repaid a Tarun loan. A question describing a first-time borrower seeking ₹15 lakh is not answered by Tarun Plus on the plain limit alone.

Stand-Up India requires a greenfield project, that is, the borrower's first venture. An applicant expanding an existing business does not qualify, however well the loan amount fits the ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore range.

Startup India gives recognition and benefits, not loans. Options describing Startup India as providing collateral-free loans of a stated amount are wrong; the credit link is through the Credit Guarantee Scheme and the Fund of Funds, not direct lending.
MUDRA covers non-farm, non-corporate micro enterprises, with allied agricultural activities included — but not crop loans. Treating MUDRA as a farm-credit scheme is a common error.
The DPIIT startup turnover ceiling is ₹100 crore in any financial year and the age ceiling is ten years. Distractors typically offer ₹25 crore, ₹250 crore, seven years or five years.
The margin money requirement under Stand-Up India was brought down to up to 15%; the older 25% figure still appears in dated material and is planted among the options.
ga-mudra.timeTarget: 10-15 seconds per question, since all of these are single-fact recalls, and up to 20 seconds for a loan-amount scenario where you must place a figure in a band. Learning target: one 45-minute block to build the three scheme cards, then 8 minutes of revision every fortnight.
ga-mudra.masteryCheck: In 2 minutes write out: the four MUDRA categories with exact limits and the Tarun Plus repeat-borrower condition; Stand-Up India's launch date, loan range, beneficiary rule, greenfield requirement and 15% margin; Startup India's launch date, DPIIT criteria (ten years, ₹100 crore), the Section 80-IAC benefit with its 1 April 2030 window, and the Fund of Funds link to SIDBI. Then answer 10 five-option MCQs, including at least three that give you a loan amount and ask for the scheme or category, in under 2 minutes with at most one wrong.
questionPatterns: Category placement from a loan amount — 'A loan of ₹4 lakh under PMMY falls under which category? (a) Shishu (b) Kishore (c) Tarun (d) Tarun Plus (e) None of these' — answer (b), since Kishore covers above ₹50,000 up to ₹5 lakh.

Scheme identification from a beneficiary description — a woman or SC/ST entrepreneur setting up a first venture, with MUDRA, Stand-Up India, Startup India, PMEGP and Stand-Up Mitra offered as five options.
Direct limit or criterion recall — the maximum MUDRA loan, the Stand-Up India loan range, or the DPIIT turnover ceiling, against five numeric options.

Statement-combination on Startup India — three statements about DPIIT recognition, the tax exemption period and the Fund of Funds, with five combination options such as 'Only I and II', 'All of these', 'None of these'.

Institution matching — which institution MUDRA Ltd is a subsidiary of, or which ministry runs Startup India, with SIDBI, NABARD, RBI, DPIIT and the Ministry of Finance distributed across five choices.

ga-mudra.blockPlan: One 45-minute build block plus two short recall touches. Block A (45 min): write three scheme cards side by side — MUDRA, Stand-Up India, Startup India — each with launch date, beneficiary, amount, key condition and administering body, then read across the row to feel the contrasts (beneficiary, amount range, credit versus recognition). ga-insurance.whatItIs: Insurance transfers risk from the insured to the insurer in exchange for a premium. India's sector is regulated by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, a statutory body created by the IRDA Act, 1999 with headquarters in Hyderabad. The topic splits into three parts for Mains: the principles of insurance, the institutional and regulatory facts about IRDAI and the underlying Insurance Act, 1938, and the current-affairs layer — the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025, the GST exemption of September 2025 and the Bima Trinity.
ga-insurance.coreMethod:
1. Learn the seven principles as a list with a one-line test each: utmost good faith (disclose every material fact), insurable interest (you must stand to lose), indemnity (you are restored, not enriched), subrogation (the insurer inherits your claim against the wrongdoer), contribution (multiple insurers share the loss), proximate cause (the nearest effective cause decides liability) and loss minimisation (you must act to limit the damage).
2. Attach the two standard exceptions that questions are built on: life insurance is not a contract of indemnity, because human life cannot be valued — it is a benefit or assurance contract, and subrogation and contribution do not apply to it. Insurable interest must exist at the time of taking the policy in life insurance, at the time of loss in marine insurance, and at both times in fire insurance.
3. Worked example: 'A house worth ₹40 lakh is insured for ₹40 lakh with Insurer A and ₹40 lakh with Insurer B. It is completely destroyed by fire. The maximum total amount the owner can recover is (a) ₹80 lakh (b) ₹60 lakh (c) ₹40 lakh (d) ₹20 lakh (e) Nil' — under indemnity and contribution the two insurers share the actual loss, so the answer is (c) ₹40 lakh.
4. Fix the institutional facts: IRDAI set up under the IRDA Act, 1999, headquarters Hyderabad; the current chairman is Ajay Seth, who took charge on 1 September 2025 for a three-year term; the governing statute for insurers remains the Insurance Act, 1938. LIC was formed in 1956 by nationalising life insurance; general insurance was nationalised in 1972 with GIC, which today functions as the national reinsurer after its four subsidiaries were delinked in 2002.
5. Fix the policyholder-protection numbers from IRDAI's 2024 master circular framework: the free-look period is 30 days for all policies; a death claim without investigation is to be settled within 15 days, and where investigation is required it is to be completed within 45 days with settlement within 15 days thereafter; in health insurance, cashless authorisation is to be granted within one hour of request and final discharge authorisation within three hours; the maximum pre-existing-disease waiting period is three years and the moratorium after which a claim cannot be repudiated except for fraud is five years; there is no maximum entry age for health policies. From the Insurance Act, Section 45 bars a policy from being called in question after three years.
6. Learn the current-affairs layer, which Mains rewards heavily: GST on all individual life and individual health insurance policies, including reinsurance, was reduced from 18% to nil with effect from 22 September 2025. The Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Bill, 2025 was passed by Parliament on 16-17 December 2025 and received presidential assent on 20 December 2025; it raises the FDI limit in Indian insurance companies from 74% to 100% with the requirement that one of the chairman, managing director or chief executive be an Indian citizen, reduces the net-owned-fund requirement for foreign reinsurers from ₹5,000 crore to ₹1,000 crore, and retains the minimum paid-up capital of ₹100 crore for insurers and ₹200 crore for reinsurers. Bima Sugam, the one-stop digital insurance marketplace, was launched by IRDAI on 17 September 2025; with Bima Vistaar (an affordable composite product) and Bima Vahak (a women-centric distribution channel) it forms the Bima Trinity.
7. Add the two mandatory-cover facts that recur: third-party motor insurance is compulsory under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, and PMFBY is the crop insurance scheme with farmer premium capped at 2% for kharif, 1.5% for rabi and 5% for commercial and horticultural crops.
8. In the exam, first classify: principle question, institutional-fact question or current-affairs question. Principle questions can be reasoned in ten seconds; the other two are pure recall and should be skipped if they do not surface.
tricks: Test any indemnity question by asking 'can the insured end up richer than before the loss?' If an option allows that, it is wrong. This single check settles indemnity, contribution and subrogation questions without recalling the definitions separately.

Insurable interest timing is a three-item run — life at inception, marine at loss, fire at both. Reciting 'inception, loss, both' in that order answers the whole family, and it is far cheaper than memorising three separate rules.

Life insurance is the exception to almost everything: not indemnity, no subrogation, no contribution. When a five-option question asks which principle does NOT apply to life insurance, you are choosing among indemnity, subrogation and contribution, which cuts the field immediately.

The FDI sequence in Indian insurance is 26% then 49% then 74% then 100%. Holding it as an ascending run makes 'the limit was raised from what to what' questions instant, and the current answer is 74 to 100 under the 2025 Act.

Group the 2025 insurance current-affairs items by month — GST exemption from 22 September 2025, Bima Sugam launched 17 September 2025, the amendment Act assented 20 December 2025, Ajay Seth taking charge 1 September 2025. Learning them as an autumn-to-winter 2025 sequence makes the dates mutually reinforcing.
traps: Life insurance is not a contract of indemnity. Because most textbook examples of insurance are property-based, candidates over-generalise indemnity to life cover, and the question is set precisely to catch that.

The Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha Act, 2025 did not itself introduce a composite licence permitting one insurer to write all classes; it retains the existing class-based registration and only provides an enabling framework for the government to notify such a regime later. Options claiming composite licensing is now in force overstate the Act.

GST was reduced to nil on individual life and individual health policies from 22 September 2025 — this is an exemption for individual policies, not a blanket removal of GST from every insurance product. Do not extend it to all general insurance.
IRDAI's headquarters is Hyderabad, not Mumbai. Mumbai is the headquarters of RBI and SEBI, and the option is placed there to exploit the association.
The free-look period is 30 days for all policies under the current framework; the older 15-day figure for non-distance marketing is superseded and still appears among the distractors.

The minimum paid-up capital was retained at ₹100 crore for insurers and ₹200 crore for reinsurers by the 2025 Act — it was not reduced. What was reduced was the net-owned-fund requirement for foreign reinsurers, from ₹5,000 crore to ₹1,000 crore. These two facts are routinely swapped in options.
ga-insurance.timeTarget: 10 seconds for a principle question you can reason, 12-15 seconds for an institutional fact, and up to 20 seconds for a statement-combination question on the 2025 reforms. Learning target: one 50-minute block split between principles and institutions, plus a 15-minute current-affairs refresh in the month before Mains.
ga-insurance.masteryCheck: In 2 minutes write out: the seven principles with a one-line test each, marked to show which three do not apply to life insurance; the insurable-interest timing run; IRDAI's founding Act, year, headquarters and current chairman; the free-look, death-claim and cashless-authorisation time limits; and the four 2025 items — GST nil from 22 September, Bima Sugam launch, the FDI change to 100%, and the ₹100 crore / ₹200 crore capital retention. Then answer 12 five-option MCQs mixing principles with 2025 current affairs in under 3 minutes, at most two wrong.
questionPatterns: Principle application through a short scenario — double insurance, an over-insured asset, or an insurer recovering from a third party after paying a claim, with the seven principles distributed across five options.

Exception identification — 'Which of the following principles does NOT apply to a life insurance contract? (a) Utmost good faith (b) Insurable interest (c) Indemnity (d) Proximate cause (e) Loss minimisation' — answer (c), since life cover is a benefit contract, not one of indemnity.
Institutional recall — IRDAI's establishing Act and year, its headquarters, its current chairman, or the year of LIC or GIC formation, each against five choices.

Current-affairs recall on the 2025 reforms — the new FDI ceiling, the effective date of the GST exemption, the name of the amendment Act, or what Bima Sugam is, with five descriptive or numeric options.

Statement-combination on policyholder protection — three statements about the free-look period, claim settlement timelines and the health moratorium, with five combination options such as 'Only I and III', 'All of these', 'None of these'.
